news.title: Ruby Rippey, former Gavin Newsom staffer, offers new details on their affair 20 years ago
news.text:
SAN FRANCISCO -- A former staffer who had an affair with Gavin Newsom more than 20 years ago offered extensive details in an essay published Tuesday by Vanity Fair, taking issue with how the California governor has more recently characterized what happened.

Newsom, then the mayor of San Francisco, admitted in 2007 that he had an affair in the years prior with Ruby Rippey, his appointments secretary and the wife of his campaign manager, Alex Tourk. Rippey has not spoken much about the scandal as Newsom has risen in politics and emerged as a potential 2028 presidential contender.

In the Vanity Fair piece, Rippey criticizes Newsom's description of the affair and its fallout in a memoir he published earlier this year. He wrote that it was the "briefest of affairs," and recounted how he "came clean" to Tourk, a close friend.

"That detail-subtle but significant-is the one that stays with me," Rippey wrote. "It reads-to me, at least-as a version of events that gives him credit for something I had already done."

Newsom had filed for divorce from his wife, former Fox News host Kimberly Guilfoyle, before the affair, but the relationship with his subordinate was an early political stumbling block for Newsom. Tourk resigned after confronting Newsom about it, and Newsom later held a news conference where he said, "Everything you've read is true and I'm deeply sorry for that."

Still, he was reelected later that year with over 73% of the vote.

"The Governor acknowledged his role and publicly apologized nearly two decades ago when he was still mayor," Newsom spokesperson Izzy Gardon said in a statement to CNN and KGO-TV/ABC7 Eyewitness News in San Francisco, responding to Rippey's essay.

"In the time since, he met his wife, started a family, and has focused on serving Californians. He addressed this chapter of his life, including in his memoir, and out of respect for everyone involved, does not have anything further to add," the statement said.

Newsom's personal life is likely to come under more scrutiny if he runs for president in 2028.

The governor, who has since married Jennifer Siebel Newsom, has been open about his interest in a possible White House bid as he has urged fellow Democrats to stand up more to President Donald Trump and "fight fire with fire."

Writing for Vanity Fair, Rippey traces the start of the affair to the summer of 2005 and said it coincided with a period in her life when she was struggling with alcohol addiction. She said she was accountable for her actions but noted that the #MeToo movement, which started in 2017, opened her eyes to the power imbalance in their relationship.

"Both things are true: I am responsible for what I did. Power does not distribute consequences evenly," Rippey, now sober, wrote. "For my former boss, it is a footnote in a longer arc of ascent. For me, it is the fracture that split my life into before and after."

She said she considered whether to speak out publicly in the aftermath of the affair and was approached about writing a memoir. But she credited Kamala Harris, then the San Francisco district attorney, with giving her the best advice she received.

"I wouldn't say anything right now, Ruby. Just pause. More time will give you better perspective," she said Harris told her.

CNN has reached out to a Harris representative for comment.

news.title: The DNC Is a Broke, Phone-Throwing Mess With a Kamala Harris Hangover
news.text:
Last week I wrote about the fact that the Democratic Party is having serious money problems. In every case you can look at, the party is way behind the fundraising of comparable groups on the Republican side of the aisle. But the situation is particularly grim for the DNC which isn't just behind in fundraising; it's actually in the red. 

The DNC ended June with $16.3 million in cash and $18.5 million in debt — putting it about $2.2 million in the red. It is a staggering hole compared to the numbers of the Republican National Committee, which held $128.5 million and reported no debt.For months, Martin and his allies have predicted that Democratic victories and the approaching midterms would bring major donors back. The midterms are now approaching. The money has not followed.

As Ed pointed out yesterday, we don't even know how bad the situation really is because the DNC has been asking vendors not to bill them until after the midterms. So there may be more debt out there that we don't know about and won't until sometime in December.

In the center of this mess is Ken Martin. Martin is apparently struggling with the failure of the DNC to the point that he is now being internally investigated for throwing a phone at someone.

Mr. Martin’s fraying nerves are showing. In a pique of frustration in early July, he threw his phone at the desk of a junior aide while upbraiding the person. The phone-tossing incident resulted in a formal complaint to the D.N.C.’s human resources department.The fallout from the phone-throwing episode was described by half a dozen people familiar with the incident, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss internal party matters. None of them witnessed the encounter, and there was some dispute over how aggressively the phone was tossed. Mr. Martin was said to have thrown the phone at the desk, rather than at the aide.Mr. Martin later met with D.N.C. human resources officials about his behavior, according to three of the people.

In addition to being irrationally angry, Martin is also said to be increasingly paranoid.

Even supporters acknowledge Mr. Martin’s growing sense of paranoia. He confronted the party’s finance director this spring over what he thought was a budding coup. And before he met with the top congressional Democrats, Senator Chuck Schumer of New York and Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, in mid-July, assurances were given to an ally of Mr. Martin’s that the two party leaders did not plan to use the gathering to call for the chairman’s resignation.

Martin wrote a lengthy defense of his tenure but ultimately no one can overlook the fact that the DNC is broke just months before the midterms. And that means it won't be offering any help to candidates who might need it.

For more than a decade, the D.N.C. has transferred millions of dollars every election to sister committees responsible for winning the House and Senate. But the national party is now so short on cash — even after taking out a $15 million loan last year — that officials have privately conveyed to congressional leadership that there will be no such transfers in 2026.

That $15 million taken out last year is the largest loan the DNC has ever taken out. And as NOTUS reported recently, it used its own headquarters as collateral.

The Democratic National Committee put its physical headquarters up for collateral last year in order to obtain a $15 million line of credit to help invest in off-year elections, according to D.C. deed records not previously reported.

How perfectly symbolic would it be if the DNC got evicted and wound up homeless. It's probably not possible. I assume someone in Hollywood would step up to rescue them before that happened. Still, the fact that they are absolutely broke three months before an election that, in many ways, ought to favor Democrats, is remarkable. Part of the problem is the Kamala Harris hangover.

Some of the problems are a hangover from 2024. While Vice President Kamala Harris raised record sums that year, her loss left many big Democratic donors disillusioned with the party. Her campaign also had millions in debt that the D.N.C. spent much of last year paying off, with Ms. Harris’s help...The single biggest expense in the Martin era was $7.3 million to buy the remnants of Ms. Harris’s campaign list from her failed 2024 bid. Ms. Harris’s political action committee used the money to cover additional remaining debts.

That's why they needed the $15 million loan last year. And they haven't recovered since then. The flood of money that Martin predicted never came. Now it's probably too late.

Rippey, who was married to Newsom's campaign manager at the time, Alex Tourk, and who served as the mayor's appointments secretary, disclosed that Harris, who, at the time was the San Francisco District Attorney, privately advised Rippey to "pause" and refrain from public comment or taking a book deal as the scandal broke. "She listens, then says simply: ‘I wouldn’t say anything right now, Ruby. Just pause. More time will give you better perspective,’" Rippey claims Harris told her after the affair became public. Rippey notes that Newsom’s book wrongly claims he was the one who "came clean" to her husband, a detail she says gives him credit for a confession she had already made. When she asked a Newsom advisor if the governor "tells the truth" in the book, he responded, "Well, we all remember things differently, don’t we, Ruby?" Rippey described beginning the affair while working at City Hall, detailing encounters that included sitting in a hot tub together, spending nights in hotel rooms, and visiting his Russian Hill penthouse. He is in the front seat. He takes one of my feet and begins to massage it, the gesture half-hidden inside the loud car." news.title: Daughter of late House Dem forced into runoff after falling short in special election
news.text: Marcye Scott, the daughter of late Rep. David Scott, D-Ga., and former Gwinnett County school board chair Everton Blair advanced Tuesday to an Aug. 25 runoff in the special election to serve the remainder of the late Congressman Scott's term before the winner of November’s regular election takes office for a full-term beginning in January. Neither candidate captured the 50% majority needed to win the seat outright, according to the Associated Press, which called the race around a quarter to 9 o'clock East Coast time. Scott had received 47.5% of the vote and Blair had received 36.1% when the race was called around 8:45 p.m. eastern, with 85% of the expected vote counted. Republican Caesar Gonzales was far behind in third with just 8.5%. The runoff will determine who serves the final weeks of the late-Congressman's term in the heavily Democratic metro Atlanta 13th Congressional District following his death in April at age 80. It will not determine who represents the district for the next full two-year term beginning in January; voters held a separate primary for that term in May, with the general election set for Nov. 3. SUCCESSION: WHY CONGRESS HAS NO CLEAR PLAN WHEN LAWMAKERS CAN’T SERVE Democratic state Rep. Jasmine Clark won the regularly scheduled May primary for the full term with roughly 56% of the vote and will face Republican Jonathan Chavez in November. Blair, the only special-election candidate who also competed in that regular May primary, finished third with approximately 12%. Regardless of party affiliation, all candidates appeared together on one special-election ballot Tuesday. Georgia law allows a candidate who receives more than 50% to win outright, but sends the two leading candidates to a runoff when no one reaches that mark. Six names appeared on the ballot, although Democrat Tony Brown was disqualified after the check he submitted for the $5,220 qualifying fee bounced, according to the Georgia Secretary of State’s Office, which indicated votes cast for Brown would not count. The remaining field included Scott, Blair Gonzales, Attorney Carlos Moore and Republican candidate Fayth Park. Scott announced during her father’s early-May funeral in Atlanta that she planned to run in the special election to complete his term. Scott has cast herself as the candidate best positioned to complete her father’s unfinished work, particularly his outstanding federal funding requests, with her campaign noting how she worked alongside her father for more than two decades, playing an active role in his campaign operations, fundraising, constituent outreach and community engagement. 100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY "Right after my dad passed, a lot of the City Council or the commissioners and chair people, they wanted to know what was going to happen with these projects," Scott said following her father's death, according the Atlanta-Journal Constitution. "And that’s really why I’m running: to complete that." Her runoff opponent, Blair, was elected to the Gwinnett County Board of Education in 2018 and was elected board chairman a few years later in 2021. According to Blair's campaign website, the former high school math teacher earned a bachelor’s degree in applied mathematics and a doctorate in education leadership from Harvard University, as well as a master’s degree in policy, organization and leadership from Stanford University. Blair’s campaign has highlighted that education-policy background and his prior elected service on the Gwinnett County school board. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The winner of the August runoff will add another Democratic vote to a narrowly divided House. Republicans officially hold 218 seats, compared with 212 Democrats and four vacancies, while independent Rep. Kevin Kiley of California continues to caucus with Republicans despite defecting from the GOP earlier this year. Once the Georgia winner is sworn in, Democrats would hold 213 seats, compared with a 219-member Republican-aligned bloc. The 13th District includes portions of Clayton, DeKalb, Gwinnett, Henry and Newton counties, along with all of Rockdale County. David Scott carried the district with approximately 72% of the vote in 2024. In the presidential race that same year, then-Vice President Kamala Harris received roughly 71% of the district’s vote, compared with about 28% for President Donald Trump.
news.summary: Marcye Scott and Gwinnett County school board chair Everton Blair advance to an Aug. 25 Georgia special election runoff in the 13th District for a House seat.

news.title: Adam Schiff’s attack on free speech is a parody of itself
news.text:
Adam Schiff wants to ban AI parodies of political candidates. The irony runs deep.

Recall that when Schiff impeached President Donald Trump in 2019, he made up a fake version of Trump’s phone call with Ukraine’s President Volodymr Zelensky.

When Republicans complained that Schiff had misrepresented the actual conversation, which was the core of his charge against Trump, Schiff claimed it was just a “parody.” No one was laughing — but that was his excuse. 

Now Schiff is introducing a bill that would ban “misrepresentation through the use of content generated in whole or in part with the use of artificial intelligence” in political campaign ads.

It’s the second time Schiff has tried to suppress free speech this way — and it repeats the effort by California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who signed similar legislation in 2024 to protect Kamala Harris from AI “deep fake” parodies.

A federal judge threw out Newsom’s legislation last year, pointing out that it infringed on “constitutionally protected speech.” The judge added, wryly, that forcing AI-generated parodies to add disclaimers — which Schiff’s legislation also wants to do — “would kill the joke.”

At least Newsom made a feeble effort to acknowledge parody as a legitimate use of AI. Schiff’s legislation has no carveout for parody. It is as humorless as the man himself. 

Schiff’s partner in this absurd effort is none other than Rep. Ro Khanna, a Democrat who knows the meaning of defamation — which is why he falsely accused several men of ties to Jeffrey Epstein in February.

Schiff likes to preen as a champion of free speech — when he’s defending Jimmy Kimmel.

But when it comes to everyone else’s speech — including AI videos that poke fun at Schiff and his colleagues — Schiff is suddenly eager to be the censor and to attach disclaimers to comedy and commentary.

There is a reason Democrats are trying to revive an idea that the courts have already killed, and it has a name: Spencer Pratt.

Pratt’s run for mayor of LA earlier this year inspired many creators to publish AI-generated videos mocking incumbent Mayor Karen Bass and Newsom.

Though Pratt’s campaign did not create these ads, they went viral and helped elevate his profile to the national level.

Anyone can make AI parodies, but conservatives have the edge, for the moment. That is why Schiff is making his move.

It’s a mockery of the First Amendment. Call it a parody.

news.title: California Dems target AI campaign ads after Spencer Pratt and Steve Hilton’s viral political attacks
news.text:
Two California Democrats have have called on Congress to slam the brakes on Hollywood-style AI campaign ads just as they become the norm for political campaigns. 

US Sen. Adam Schiff and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont) on Monday reintroduced the “AI Ads Act,” which is seeking to ban the fraudulent use of artificial intelligence to impersonate political candidates or committees in federal campaigns as AI-generated election content becomes more sophisticated.

The push comes just days after Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton unveiled a pair of AI-generated campaign ads attacking Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra. 

One featured a riff on the “Gladiator” franchise while the other pit Hilton against a “machine” supposedly representing Democratic Party’s grip on California politics.

Those videos followed a string of viral AI videos created by the campaign of former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt. 

The ex-reality TV villain turned candidate was buoyed by the work of Los Angeles director Charles Curran, whose “Pratt Man” video riffed on the “Batman” franchise and led to millions of views.

Schiff, who originally introduced the legislation while serving in the House of Representatives, said the issue is non-partisan even if Republicans seem to have wielded AI-driven campaign videos to greater effect.

“AI-generated fraudulent advertising which uses the likeness or voices of candidates to misrepresent their positions, campaigns, or causes, or otherwise misrepresents a candidate’s point of view is not only wrong — it poses a serious threat to our democracy that should concern all Americans regardless of their party,” Schiff said.

Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters 

The bill would amend the Federal Election Campaign Act to explicitly prohibit fraudulent misrepresentation through content generated wholly or partly by artificial intelligence. 

It would also broaden existing federal prohibitions by applying them to anyone falsely claiming to represent a candidate or political organization — and eliminate the requirement that a misrepresentation be shown to be “damaging” before enforcement could occur. 

The proposal closely tracks bipartisan recommendations issued by the Federal Election Commission in 2022 to modernize campaign fraud laws.

Khanna, a likely presidential candidate in 2028, said artificial intelligence should not be “used to mislead voters or undermine our democracy.”

Unlike many of the “deepfake” concerns driving lawmakers, the Hilton and Pratt videos relied on clearly fictional, stylized animation rather than realistic fabricated footage designed to appear authentic. 

The AI Ads Act targets fraudulent impersonation of candidates or political organizations, including AI-generated content used to deceive voters or solicit campaign donations under false pretenses, rather than banning AI-generated political advertising altogether.

The legislation is backed by Common Cause, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, Campaign Legal Center, Protect Democracy and Public Citizen.

More than 30 states have adopted laws addressing deceptive AI-generated election content, according to supporters of the measure, but Congress has yet to establish comparable nationwide standards for federal campaigns.

The bill’s prospects remain uncertain in a closely divided Congress, where lawmakers have repeatedly struggled to agree on broader AI regulations despite bipartisan concerns over the technology’s growing role in elections.
news.summary: Hollywood-style AI campaign ads have been proliferating across the national political landscape, leading two California Democrats to call on Congress to slam the brakes before cinematic deepfakes become the norm in American elections.

news.title: CBS' '60 minutes' announces new slate of correspondents for upcoming 59th season
news.text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Two months after a major shakeup, CBS’s “60 Minutes” has hired a lineup of new correspondents and contributors in time for its 59th season, including Ross Douthat, a conservative opinion columnist at The New York Times, and Norah O’Donnell, former anchor of “CBS Evening News.”

The show’s new executive producer, Nick Bilton, announced the news in a staff memo Tuesday, shared on X. Joining Douthat and O’Donnell will be author Sebastian Junger, Trevor Phillips and Gianna Toboni. All will be contributors to the show.

The new journalists join current correspondents Lesley Stahl, Jon Wertheim and Bill Whitaker. Their hirings come two months after a shakeup at the storied program, led by the network’s new editor-in-chief, Bari Weiss.

Weiss installed Bilton, who has little substantive broadcast news experience, as executive producer, replacing Tanya Simon, who was let go after a 30-plus year tenure with the show. Also let go were correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega — and soon after, Scott Pelley, after a tense confrontation with his bosses over the changes.

In addition to the three dismissed, Anderson Cooper — whose primary job is at CNN — said earlier this year he was leaving of his own accord after two decades.

CBS News leaders enthused about the hires

Weiss and Tom Cibrowski, the CBS News president, praised the new hires in an internal memo. “We couldn’t be more excited about this news,” the two said, welcoming the new additions. “Onward!”

Bilton called Douthat “one of the preeminent public intellectuals in America today, a thinker of uncommon rigor and a journalist of deep empathy.” The columnist has spent nearly two decades at the Times and is an author of numerous books.

The producer called O’Donnell “a powerhouse.”

“You’ve seen her all over the network. She’s launched a new podcast. And you’ll see much more of her in our halls because Norah will be a correspondent on 60 Minutes.”

Bilton praised Junger for his nonfiction work “The Perfect Storm,” about a catastrophic 1991 storm. The book “landed with an electric charge in the world of reported nonfiction, defining an intense and intimate form of storytelling and establishing Sebastian as a generational talent,” Bilton said.

Toboni joins“60 Minutes” as a contributor and CBS News as a national correspondent. Previously a senior correspondent with VICE News and VICE on HBO, she comes to the program from CNN.

Calling her a journalist of “extraordinary range,” Bilton noted that Toboni has interviewed members of ISIS, investigated cartel violence in Mexico and has written a book on the death penalty.

Also serving as contributor will be Trevor Phillips, announced last month as the news division’s senior global affairs correspondent. Based in London, he is “one of the most respected and trusted voices in the United Kingdom for his ability to ask the toughest questions and hold anyone in power to account,” Bilton wrote in his memo.

‘60 Minutes’ has faced upheaval for a while

Turmoil had raged at “60 Minutes” for more than a year before the May shakeup. Much of it came after President Donald Trump sued the show over its editing of a 2024 interview with then-Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

That became part of a broader shakeup at CBS News after Weiss was named to the new role of editor-in-chief by parent company Paramount late last year following David Ellison’s arrival as the network’s corporate leader.

Jocelyn Noveck covers the intersection of media and entertainment for The Associated Press.

news.title: Polls close in Georgia as voters decide successor in special election
news.text: The polls have closed in Georgia as two races in politically disparate parts of the country set the stage for one of the most unusual split-screen election days of the year on Tuesday. Rep. David Scott’s death in April at age 80 created a vacancy in a heavily blue district encompassing the southern and eastern Atlanta suburbs of Stockbridge, Conyers and Snellville. With the general election ballot already decided, Tuesday’s contest will determine who will finish out Scott’s term. Scott was notably related by marriage to Braves slugger Hank Aaron. Across the country in South Dakota, Republicans vying for the Mount Rushmore State’s safely red governor’s seat have created the state's first gubernatorial runoff between incumbent Gov. Larry Rhoden and self-made millionaire bitcoin investor Toby Doeden. Kristi Noem to be Homeland Security secretary in his second term. He was unable to garner enough support in the June primary to secure the nomination outright in his first statewide election as governor. South Dakota’s runoff is expected to be a classic establishment-versus-outsider race, with Rhoden heavily favored in the polls but Doeden hoping for a Sioux Falls-fueled upset. Richard Kneip served nearly two terms before President Jimmy Carter nominated him as ambassador to Singapore. Gov. Harvey Wollman completed the final six months of Kneip’s term, and is the state’s last Democrat to hold the office. EX-NFL LINEBACKER POISED TO RETURN TO CONGRESS AFTER TEXAS RUNOFF WIN WITH JASMINE CROCKETT ENDORSEMENT Shifting back to the Deep South, Georgia Democrats are expected to hold Scott’s seat in the fall by a wide margin. Efforts to replace Scott grew in recent months, particularly among the party's progressive wing, as the 12-term, often-combative lawmaker drew increasing frustration from Democrats. That demeanor was similar to what led Everton Blair to launch his primary bid against Scott, in what his campaign page calls a "voice for a new generation." Blair previously told Fox News Digital it was a run-in with Scott at a Gwinnett County town hall, where the lawmaker gave insufficient answers to questions and then reportedly became confrontational, that led him to explore a bid. Blair had said he would "love to just hear a little bit more of the congressional and legislative strategy, congressman, that you have for this administration, particularly as it pertains to safeguarding federal funds," according to Semafor, when Scott replied "hold on," before becoming agitated: "I don’t know who sent y’all, but we got these folks here who are providing answers. And I’m doing this. That’s what I’m doing," Scott said, according to the outlet. Blair responded by launching a primary bid, while remarking to Fox News Digital at the time that two other elderly Democratic members had recently died in office "at a time when every vote counts." The wave of millennial candidates seeking to replace aging Democrats was at the time dubbed the "Biden effect" — Democratic lawmakers retiring or facing potential primary challenges following the octogenarian Delawarean’s disastrous debate performance, which led to his decision to step aside for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. "That is my thing, is to finish out his year strongly, make sure that this money gets down to the district, and just make sure the 13th district is taken care of, constituency-wise, and making sure the projects go into finalization," she told the Georgia Recorder, while adding she would retain her father’s staff locally and at the Capitol for added stability. "[W]hen he first got into politics, I wasn’t even born, so I ran for some type of office or campaign every two years of my life, so this is just my norm, I’m just picking up where we left off with him," she told the outlet. A third candidate, former Mississippi judge Carlos Moore, also criticized Rep. Scott’s tenure, telling the Mississippi Free Press he wants to be a "leader who actually shows up." Moore had been suspended from the bench for one year in 2024 after a bar tribunal found he mishandled a wrongful death settlement, according to the outlet. news.title: LIVE RESULTS: GA Special House Election, SD Gubernatorial Runoff
news.text:
As if this midterm primary cycle hasn't provided us enough drama! Tonight we have two special contests that will perhaps signal the drift of the overall electorate, but at least will provide us some excitement ahead of next week's full primary slates in Michigan, Kansas, and a Senate primary in Virginia that might prove interesting.

First up is Georgia, where an all-in special election takes place today that will (possibly) fill the House seat left empty by the death of Democrat David Scott in April. Six candidates are vying to replace Scott, four Democrats and two Republicans, but Georgia election law requires a majority-vote winner. The six-way race and the short run-up to the special election make it less likely that this special election will be settled tonight. If not, Georgia will hold a runoff election next month between the top two vote-getters. 

Republicans can hope for a miracle, but shouldn't plan on one. GA-13 sits on the southeast side of the Atlanta metropolitan area, and it has a Cook index of D+21. In the district's 24-year history, only one Republican made it to 40 percent, and that was in the first election after the district's creation for the 2002 election. The last Republican presidential candidate to score 40 percent in this district was Mitt Romney, barely. Kamala Harris won 71 percent of the vote two years ago. It'd be a miracle for a Republican to make it onto a runoff ballot, and even if a Republican won, he'd get the boot in January when Democrats organize better for the November general election.

The outlook brightens in South Dakota, where Republicans will pick their gubernatorial nominee in a runoff. It's a closed primary, thankfully, so no Operation Chaos will be in play. South Dakota Searchlight sets up the contest:

Gov. Larry Rhoden and Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden are the last Republican candidates standing after a four-way primary on June 2. Nobody reached the legal threshold to win that election — the first time that's happened since lawmakers approved a state law in 1985 requiring a top-two runoff when nobody reaches 35% in primaries for governor, U.S. House and U.S. Senate. Previously when no candidate received 35%, delegates at state political party conventions chose the nominee. ...The scramble for the Republican nomination started in January 2025 when then-Gov. Kristi Noem resigned to accept a job in President Donald Trump's administration. Rhoden was Noem's lieutenant governor and was automatically promoted to serve the last two years of her second term.

Doeden actually finished first, a shock as observers expected Rep. Dusty Johnson to win the primary. Johnson tumbled to third instead, while Rhoden finished six points back of Doeden for second place. However, the only poll listed at RealClearPolling since the first round comes from Emerson, and it puts Rhoden up almost 2:1 over Doeden, 62/32. Interestingly, Donald Trump has not made an endorsement in this race, so perhaps it's closer than it appears. 

Follow the results tonight with our partners at Decision Desk HQ, providing live results in both races today. Next Tuesday, we'll have a lot more races to watch, especially the Democrat primary in Michigan for the U.S. Senate.

news.title: Kamala Harris told me to keep quiet about my affair with Gavin Newsom, says staffer
news.text:
Kamala Harris advised one of Gavin Newsom's aides not to speak publicly about an affair with her boss, the woman claimed.

Ruby Rippey said that the former vice-president told her to "just pause" about the 2005 fling with Mr Newsom, the California governor, who was mayor of San Francisco at the time.

Speaking publicly about her affair for the first time, Ms Rippey wrote in Vanity Fair that she welcomed the advice and waited until now to speak out.

When she had the affair Ms Rippey was married to a man who also worked for Mr Newsom.

She has accused the governor of lying in his biography about coming clean to her husband, stating that it was in fact she who confessed.

The affair with Ms Rippey nearly ended public life for Mr Newsom, 58, who is widely expected to run for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028.

At the time he had yet to finalise his divorce from Kimberly Guilfoyle, his first wife, now the US ambassador to Greece, and he had to publicly admit his wrongdoing.

Ms Rippey, 54, was Mr Newsom's appointments secretary and was married to Alex Tourk, his top aide.

In her first-person essay, Ms Rippey said that in 2004 she first began to notice Mr Newsom "looking at me" and one time he told her that "you look really good".

To catch his eye more often, she began to wear Chanel makeup, a yellow silk dress and pink patent leather heels to the office.

The following July, at a wedding for a City Hall staffer, things became physical.

Ms Rippey said that Mr Newsom's attention was like "oxygen" for her, writing: "There is sex, but it isn't the point. The point is proximity – to power…it isn't love. It isn't romance. It's intoxication."

At one point, Mr Newsom tried to break the affair off while scrubbing a red wine stain out of the carpet.

Looking frustrated, he turned to Ms Rippey and said: "You know, we really can't do this anymore. You can't be doing this to Alex."

Ms Rippey said that in 2007, she confessed to her husband, who left her. After she quit her job, Mr Newsom held a press conference admitting the affair and the scandal began.

'I wouldn't say anything right now, Ruby'

At that point, Ms Rippey got the call from Ms Harris, who was San Francisco's district attorney at the time.

Ms Rippey writes: "She listens, then says simply, 'I wouldn't say anything right now, Ruby. Just pause. More time will give you a better perspective'.

"It turns out to be the best advice I receive. I am newly sober and still inside the wreckage – unable to make sense of anything, let alone speak clearly about it."

Earlier this year Ms Rippey was contacted by an old colleague from the San Francisco mayor's office, who now works for Mr Newsom. They wanted to tell her that the affair would be appearing in the governor's forthcoming memoir.

When Ms Rippey asked if Mr Newsom told the truth, the aide said: "Well, we all remember things differently, don't we, Ruby?"

Ms Rippey writes that she objects to Mr Newsom saying in his book that he "came clean" to Mr Tourk.

She wrote: "It reads as a version of events that gives him credit for something I had already done. Technically defensible, perhaps, but one that leaves the unmistakable impression that he, not I, was the one who told Alex the truth".

In 2008, Mr Newsom married his second wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom, with whom he has four children.

Izzy Gardon, a spokesman for Mr Newsom, said: "The governor acknowledged his role and publicly apologised for his conduct nearly two decades ago when he was still mayor.

"In the time since, he met his wife, started a family and has focused on serving Californians."

"He addressed this chapter of his life, including in his memoir, and out of respect for everyone involved, does not have anything further to add".

The Telegraph has contacted Ms Harris's office for comment.

news.title: Secret Joe Biden Audio Tapes Released as Ex-Prez Appears to Struggle to Speak About 'Classified' Docs
news.text:
A batch of audio recordings that Joe Biden attempted to keep private has now been released to the public, RadarOnline.com can reveal, and it has pulled back the curtain on the now-former president.

The recordings, about 70 hours' worth, were made by Biden's ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer, who assisted in the publication of his 2017 book, Promise Me, Dad: A Year of Hope, Hardship, and Purpose.Joe Biden on Tape: 'This Is Classified'Biden, who kept classified information in his home, is heard telling Zwonitzer in a recording, "Some of this may be classified... So, be careful. I'm not sure ... It's not marked classified but –"

"The next thing I have here is, um, this is classified..." the now 83-year-old says at another point in the recording. In the clips, Biden also appears to be struggling to remember things, as he pauses and has issues finding the right words.

While running for a second term, Biden was criticized for stumbling over words and appearing to lose track of his thoughts, which was made evident during his disastrous debate performance against opponent Donald Trump in June 2024. He would eventually be replaced by his running mate, Kamala Harris.

In the newly released recordings, Biden again seems out of it as he asks Zwonitzer, "Alright – what was I going to ask you? Something else… Uh… um. Oh gosh. I can't think of anything else."Audio Recordings DetailsThe recordings also include Biden discussing potentially classified meetings, and "a big meeting with the CIA and everyone," "a big meeting down in the Situation Room," as well as "a long meeting where DOD brief … POTUS."

According to one clip, recorded on October 10, 2016, Biden claims he has notes that the White House was not aware of at the time: "I have extensive notes over this period of time… They didn't know I have this," he says on the tape.

In another recording, just four months later, Biden is heard saying, "I just found all the classified stuff downstairs." Another portion of the recordings has Biden trying to recall his previous conversation with his ghostwriter.

"It's confusing me," Biden is heard saying before an assistant attempted to put him back on track.Joe Biden's Legal Team RespondsThe tapes became a focal point after Justice Department special counsel Robert Hur noted them in a February 2024 report on Biden's handling of classified documents. Hur zeroed in on the documents after some information marked classified, dating back to his time as President Obama's vice president, was found in his home and private office.

After a two-year battle to keep the tapes private and several adverse rulings, Biden's lawyers relented. 

"President Biden's conversations for a book a decade ago that discussed his late son are private, and were provided to the Department of Justice on the express condition they stay that way," spokesperson TJ Ducklo said in response to the tapes being released.

"Reversing course and making them public is just the latest example of this Administration weaponizing the DOJ for political retribution. It's wrong, and while President Biden disagrees with today's decision, he also respects the courts and the vital role an independent judiciary plays in a healthy democracy."Hur, who decided not to prosecute Biden, previously said of his decision, "Mr. Biden's recorded conversations with Zwonitzer from 2017 are often painfully slow, with Mr. Biden struggling to remember events and straining at times to read and relay his own notebook entries."

He added at the time, "For these jurors, Mr. Biden's apparent lapses and failures in February and April 2017 will likely appear consistent with the diminished faculties and faulty memory he showed in Zwonitzer's interview recordings and in our interview of him."

Biden, who will be releasing another memoir, Promise Me, America, later this year, was recently seen "mumbling to himself" while at Obama's presidential center opening. He was later seen remaining on stage near the podium after much of the ceremony had ended, as he scanned the audience.

"Where's my granddaughter?" he eventually called out. Biden is currently battling stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.
news.summary: Secret audio recordings of Joe Biden speaking to his ghostwriter have been released, and he discusses classified documents.

news.title: Ex-aide who had affair with Newsom reflects on power imbalance in new essay
news.text:
In an essay for Vanity Fair published Tuesday, a former aide to Gavin Newsom reflected on the affair she had with him in the early 2000s when he was mayor of San Francisco — and on the inherent imbalance of power that shaped both the relationship and its fallout.

“Power does not need to coerce. It only needs to exist,” Ruby Rippey wrote. “The responsibility to hold the line belongs to the one who holds it. That didn’t happen. But I didn’t stumble into the space left open—I saw a possibility and went for it. Both things are true: I am responsible for what I did. Power does not distribute consequences evenly.”

Rippey, who worked for Newsom initially as a deputy campaign finance director and then as his commission secretary after he took office in 2004, wrote about her alcohol addiction, her relationship with Newsom while she was married to Newsom’s then-deputy chief of staff Alex Tourk and what happened after the news of the affair became public in 2007.

“Nearly everyone seemed to know except the one person who most needed to know: my husband,” Rippey wrote. “I had been sleeping with his boss, who was also mine, and the mayor of San Francisco.”

Rippey said the affair with Newsom began after a colleague’s wedding in July 2005 in Napa Valley. (Newsom, now governor of California, had filed for divorce from Kimberly Guilfoyle in January 2005.)

It isn’t love. It isn’t romance. It’s intoxication. The text message is a hit. The glance across the hallway, a hit. The risk floods my bloodstream. I walk down the corridors of City Hall—my nude stilettos striking the marble floor. He looks at me, his gaze deliberate, newly curious. It feels like oxygen.

I don’t stop to consider the consequences—not for Alex, not for myself, not for the life I am building. I am responding to the feeling. His attention lands like a high, and I follow it with a single-minded devotion.

The two continued a sexual relationship in places such as Newsom’s penthouse in Russian Hill and the W Hotel in Los Angeles, until she eventually entered rehab and confessed to her husband. The news became public in February 2007 when Newsom admitted to the affair.

“I want to make it clear that everything you’ve heard and read is true, and I’m deeply sorry about that,” Newsom said at the time. “I’ve hurt someone I care deeply about,” adding that it “is something I have to live with.”

Newsom declined to comment on the essay to MS NOW.

Rippey said former Vice President Kamala Harris, who was the district attorney at the time, advised her not to speak publicly. “It turns out to be the best advice I receive,” Rippey wrote. “I am newly sober and still inside the wreckage—unable to make sense of anything, let alone speak clearly about it.”

news.title: Trump Couldn't Hide His Excitement After Lil Wayne Praised This White House Plan
news.text:
Donald Trump was mocked on social media Tuesday after he giddily posted about rapper Lil Wayne supporting his controversial White House ballroom plans.

The rapper discussed the ballroom last week on the “Friends Keep Secrets” podcast and admitted he thought it was a good idea.

“I’m so glad to hear Trump say — when they was mad at him about building the ballroom — and he was like, because everything we do, we have to do it on the damn lawn,” he said. “So people who don’t know nothin’ hearin’ that, thinkin’ he just bein’ Trump — no, for real, I was glad to hear him saying that.”

Lil Wayne was one of the performers who commemorated the 50th anniversary of hip-hop at the vice presidential residence in September 2023, an event spearheaded by then-Vice President Kamala Harris. On the podcast, he said that performing on the lawn left him wondering, “What is this, a backyard barbecue?” 

Trump’s ballroom construction, which has demolished the East Wing of the White House, has been heavily criticized for a variety of reasons, not least because Trump reneged on his promise that the project would be entirely privately funded.

So it seems the president is desperate for any sign of public support for the boondoggle, er, ballroom — especially when it comes from a noted architecture critic a musician whose 2020 federal weapons charge he pardoned in 2021.

Many people were taken aback by how much Lil Wayne’s ballroom approval seemed to mean to Trump.

news.text: California Governor Gavin Newsom's affair returned to public attention on Tuesday after his former aide Ruby Rippey published a detailed personal account of their relationship. Writing in Vanity Fair, Rippey recounts the affair from her perspective, describing her struggles with alcoholism, the impact the relationship had on her personal life, and the events that led to the scandal becoming public in 2007. At the time, Newsom was mayor of San Francisco. Rippey worked in his administration and was married to Newsom's close friend and chief of staff, Alex Tourk. Newsom had also not yet finalized his divorce from Kimberly Guilfoyle, who is now the US ambassador to Greece. Rippey said she joined Newsom's successful mayoral campaign in 2003 alongside her husband before becoming an aide in City Hall. She wrote that Newsom later moved her office closer to his and recalled becoming increasingly conscious of her appearance. "I start paying closer attention to what I wear. Chanel makeup. Pink patent leather heels. A tight pencil skirt. I cross my legs; I feel important. It's hard to reconcile that woman with the person I would become in one short year," she wrote. She also recalled an exchange at a Mexican restaurant, where she said Newsom told her in front of her husband: "Hey—you look really good. You've lost all your pregnancy weight." Rippey, who describes herself as an alcoholic, wrote that the comment intensified her desire to drink despite trying to remain sober during the early months of Newsom's administration. According to her account, the affair began on 2 July 2005 after the two attended a wedding where she resumed drinking. She wrote that she later found herself alone with Newsom and described the encounter. "My boss and I end up in the narrow hallway outside the bathroom at the same time. We wait, across from each other," she wrote. "The space is tight. The silence stretches." She said she later remembered sitting in a hot tub with Newsom before travelling with him to a hotel, but that much of the evening remained unclear because of her intoxication. She wrote that she awoke the following morning in the hotel room after passing out. Describing the months that followed, Rippey wrote that the relationship became emotionally consuming. "It isn't love. It isn't romance. It's intoxication. The text message is a hit. The glance across the hallway, a hit. The risk floods my bloodstream," she wrote. She also recalled one occasion when, after spilling wine in Newsom's room, he told her: "You know, we really can't do this anymore. You can't be doing this to Alex." Although she believed the affair had ended, Rippey said it continued intermittently for several more months. She described additional meetings with Newsom, including another occasion in Los Angeles that she said followed an evening of drinking, after which she again had only fragmented memories of events. Rippey wrote that her alcohol use worsened during this period and later extended to cocaine. An emergency hospital visit prompted her family to intervene, and she entered rehabilitation. She said her sister contacted Newsom before treatment, telling him: "She is unwell. She is getting help. Even if she reaches out to you, it is your responsibility to say no." According to Rippey, Newsom replied: "God bless, God bless." In early 2007, Rippey said she confessed the affair to her husband in a message that read: "Just sex—on and off for months—with the mayor. It ended before rehab. I'm sorry." She wrote that Tourk then confronted Newsom, after which the affair became public and dominated headlines in San Francisco. Newsom publicly acknowledged the affair in February 2007 while in a relationship with Jennifer Siebel, now California's first partner. Rippey said she declined requests for media interviews at the time and rejected suggestions that the relationship had been non-consensual. "I was not coerced. I knew what I was doing," she wrote. Rippey also said then-San Francisco District Attorney Kamala Harris contacted her after the scandal emerged and advised her against speaking publicly immediately. "I wouldn't say anything right now, Ruby. Just pause. More time will give you better perspective," Harris told her, according to the essay. news.title: Five Biggest Bombshells from Gavin Newsom's Ex-Mistress Essay
news.text: Ruby Rippey, the former San Francisco City Hall aide whose affair with then-Mayor Gavin Newsom became one of the biggest political scandals of his career, has broken nearly two decades of silence in a personal essay for Vanity Fair, offering new details about the relationship, her struggles with addiction and the fallout that followed. The essay, published Tuesday, arrives as Newsom, now California's Democratic Governor, continues to face speculation about a potential 2028 presidential run. Rippey's account revisits the scandal that erupted in 2007 after her then-husband, Alex Tourk—one of Newsom's closest political advisers—learned of the affair. Newsom publicly acknowledged the relationship at the time and apologized. A spokesperson for Newsom told Newsweek that Rippey's essay is consistent with previous accounts about the affair and that Newsom was not in a relationship at the time. "The Governor acknowledged his role and publicly apologized nearly two decades ago when he was still mayor. In the time since, he met his wife, started a family, and has focused on serving Californians. He addressed this chapter of his life, including in his memoir, and out of respect for everyone involved, does not have anything further to add," the spokesperson said. Why Rippey's Essay Matters Now The Newsom-Rippey affair dominated California political news in 2007 because Rippey was married to Newsom's longtime adviser and campaign manager while also working under the mayor in City Hall. The scandal prompted Tourk's resignation, raised questions about workplace power dynamics, and threatened Newsom's political future. Despite the controversy, Newsom won reelection as mayor later that year and eventually rose to become governor of California. Rippey's new essay does not allege criminal wrongdoing. Instead, it offers a deeply personal recounting of addiction, recovery, shame, and the consequences of a relationship that became a defining episode in California political history. For Newsom, who remains one of the Democratic Party's highest-profile figures, the essay likely ensures renewed attention on a scandal that many observers viewed as long settled. Kamala Harris Reportedly Urged Her Not to Speak Out One of the essay's most politically significant disclosures involves former Vice President Kamala Harris. According to Rippey, Harris advised her to avoid speaking publicly about the scandal in the immediate aftermath. Rippey recalled then District Attorney Harris telling her that "more time will give you better perspective," advice she says contributed to her decision to remain largely silent for years. The recollection offers a new glimpse into how allies and associates of the key figures in the scandal responded behind the scenes as national media scrutiny intensified. Harris and Newsom emerged from the same San Francisco political world in the early 2000s and are often described by California observers as longtime political "frenemies," as figures whose careers have blended cooperation and competition. Both benefited from connections to former San Francisco Mayor Willie Brown and rose rapidly through California Democratic politics, though generally on parallel tracks rather than directly against one another. At various points, the two have publicly supported one another. Harris backed Newsom during California's 2021 recall election campaign, while Newsom became an early supporter of Harris's national political ambitions. Yet political analysts have long viewed them as potential rivals because each has been seen as a future Democratic presidential contender and they have often occupied neighboring positions within California's political hierarchy Newsweek reached out to Harris' office for comment via email. How the Affair Allegedly Began Rippey's account provides far more detail about the origins of the relationship than has previously been public. The affair occurred in 2005 while Newsom, then around 37 or 38, was separated from, or in the process of divorcing, his first wife Kimberly Guilfoyle, according to reporting at the time. The relationship became public in 2007, by which point Newsom was dating future wife Jennifer Siebel Newsom. In the essay, Rippey, who was 33, recounts flirtations that developed into a romantic relationship, describing private encounters and meetings with Newsom while both worked in San Francisco city government. She writes about events surrounding a Napa Valley wedding and other meetings that she says marked the beginning of the affair. Those details were largely absent from public reporting when the scandal first broke in 2007. 'It Wasn't Love. It Was Proximity to Power.' Perhaps the most striking theme running through Rippey's essay is her reflection on why she became involved with Newsom. Looking back, she argues the relationship was fueled less by romance than by the allure of influence and status associated with one of California's rising political stars. She writes that the experience was about feeling "chosen" and describes the attraction as connected to "proximity to power." "We meet and we drink. There is sex, but it isn’t the point. The point is proximity—to power, to being chosen, to feeling newly visible—no longer muted by pregnancy, by new motherhood, by the strain of white-knuckling long stretches of sobriety," she wrote. "It isn’t love. It isn’t romance. It’s intoxication. The text message is a hit. The glance across the hallway, a hit. The risk floods my bloodstream." Rippey's observation is likely to attract attention because it directly addresses questions that have long surrounded the power dynamics at the center of the scandal. Her Sister Allegedly Contacted Newsom During Rehab Rippey also describes severe struggles with alcohol addiction and substance abuse during the period surrounding the affair, including blackouts, medical emergencies and rehab treatment. According to her account, while she was receiving treatment, her sister contacted Newsom to explain that Rippey was "unwell" and entering recovery. Rippey writes that her sister asked the future governor not to see her again. She says Newsom's reported response was brief: "God bless." She Confessed to Her Husband in an Email Another revelation concerns how the affair was ultimately disclosed to Tourk. Rippey writes that therapists and treatment staff advised her not to tell her husband because of the potential impact on her recovery and because the matter involved a prominent public figure. She says she ultimately rejected that advice. Instead, she confessed in an email. "I still wonder which was the greater offense: my infidelity or my failure to look him in the eye when I told him about it," Rippey said. "Reading his emails to me from that time is the hardest part to revisit," she wrote later in the piece. "Not because of what he says, but because I can see the result of my actions landing on the person I loved most." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Trevor Davies

news.title: New audio undercuts Dems who defended Biden, slammed Hur after classified docs report revealed memory loss
news.text: After special counsel Robert Hur’s 2023 investigation and the subsequent report into former President Joe Biden’s retention of classified documents, Democrats rushed to defend the 46th president from his characterization that Biden was an "elderly man with a poor memory." The left-wing's narrative surrounding Biden's mental cognition — especially as he was running for re-election against President Donald Trump — is now crumbling after audio tapes from the investigation were revealed Monday night. Prominent Democrats lined up to defend Biden when the initial report was released in 2024, many using the same line that Hur's report was "gratuitous." Then-Vice President Kamala Harris was chief among the chorus of defenders, saying that the report was "inaccurate and inappropriate." "The way that the president’s demeanor in that report was characterized could not be more wrong on the facts," she told reporters at an event in Washington at the time. She also said the report was "clearly politically motivated, gratuitous." Months later, Biden dropped out of the presidential race and was replaced on the ticket by his No. 2 without a primary election to decide his replacement. BIDEN'S HUR INTERVIEW TAPES COULD NOW GO PUBLIC AFTER HIS ATTORNEYS WAVE WHITE FLAG "What everyone will soon realize is that this is a Republican special counsel who completely went out of his way to editorialize, to include material in his report that is unnecessary and irrelevant to what he was tasked with doing," Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., piled on in comments to ABC at the time. Hur's appointment was nonpartisan. In 2023, Hur was investigating Biden for retaining classified information. At the center of the investigation were audio tapes of Biden from interviews with his "Promise Me, Dad" memoir ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer, from 2016 and 2017. Hur's report concluded that Biden did, in fact, retain classified documents, but that prosecuting him might not lead to a conviction, because he could be viewed "as a sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory." "Mr. Biden's memory was significantly limited, both during his recorded interviews with the ghostwriter in 2017 and in his interview with our office in 2023," the report said. BIDEN’S FIGHT TO KEEP HUR INTERVIEW TAPES UNDER WRAPS SUFFERS FRESH COURT BLOW After a prolonged legal battle during which Biden sought to keep the audio tapes private, a nonprofit called the Oversight Project obtained them via public records requests. The damning tapes reveal Biden's inability to remember basic names and dates. In one instance, on April 24, 2017, Biden struggled to recall the names of two economic advisers. "I’ll think of his name," said Biden, who at the time was a private citizen and former vice president. "I should write the names down because I keep forgetting them." There was then a long pause before Zwonitzer prompted Biden by saying Alan Krueger’s name. BIDEN SCORES TEMPORARY COURT VICTORY AS TRUMP-APPOINTED JUDGE DELAYS RELEASE OF HUR INVESTIGATION MATERIALS In another instance, when trying to recall a memorial he attended for a fallen service member, Biden forgot the date of the service and name of the deceased. "I think I went to that memorial service in Wilmington. It says [REDACTED] December the 4th, but I don't -- I know what this means. Memorial service -- [REDACTED] gets names really f---ed up," said Biden. "So it says memorial service for [REDACTED]. I don't think her name was [REDACTED]. Or I forget [REDACTED]." The interviews were marked by consistent lapses in memory. But in 2024, that didn't stop Democrats from accusing Hur of being a partisan activist who intentionally tried to tarnish Biden and his chances in a rematch against Trump. Andrew Weissman, a former general counsel to the FBI, cried foul on MSNBC. "That is not the role of the Department of Justice ... to talk about your memory today — irrelevant, it is gratuitous," he reportedly said. "And it is also exactly what you're not supposed to do, which is putting your thumb on the scale that could have political repercussions." Ian Sams, a spokesperson for Biden's general counsel, said at the time that the report was "gratuitous." "When you are the first special counsel in history not to indict anybody, there is pressure to criticize and to make, you know, statements that maybe in otherwise you wouldn't make," Sams reportedly said. "I think this issue of age is already out there, and when November comes, it’s going to be a choice between two people," said Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., told POLITICO. "I was with a congressional leadership about two weeks ago, and no one walked out of that meeting, saying, ‘Oh, my God, it was like he wasn’t in charge.’" Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., who at the time had just spent a day traveling with Biden, insisted that he was, "at the very top of his game, all the way through it, both in private and in person." Later in 2024, Biden was yanked from the top of the presidential ticket after an embarrassing debate performance against then-candidate Donald Trump, which showcased his apparent mental decline. Harris, serving as vice president at the time, was then coronated as the party's presidential nominee despite never winning a primary. When she ran in 2020, Harris never made it to the primaries, dropping out on December 3, 2019, months before the first elections took place. news.title: Battleground Democrat flip-flops on conversion therapy after left-wing backlash
news.text: A Democratic House candidate vying to flip a key Republican-held seat is on the defensive after reversing her position on conversion therapy following backlash from the party's left flank. Rebecca Cooke, a Democratic challenger vying to unseat Rep. Derrick Van Orden, R-Wis., repeatedly declined to endorse a federal ban on conversion therapy during several forums held ahead of the Aug. 11 primary. But after drawing criticism from some progressive voters, Cooke reversed course, saying the federal government should prohibit the controversial practice, which often involves mental health professionals offering talk therapy for individuals struggling with their sexual orientation or gender identity. The issue gained renewed attention when the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that Colorado could not enforce a state-level ban on conversion therapy over free speech concerns, sparking backlash from some Democrats. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME The reversal comes as Cooke appears to be walking a political tightrope on LGBTQ issues in the Trump-friendly swing district, where she must appeal to both Democratic primary voters and the broader electorate. Before Cooke can seek a rematch against Van Orden, she must first overcome a primary challenge from former Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge, who is running to her left. Asked what lawmakers could do to push back against the Supreme Court ruling at a May forum in La Crosse, Cooke sidestepped the question and said she preferred "local communities having control." "I’m in favor of that sort of local control when making policies like this," the Wisconsin Democrat said. Wisconsin’s conversion therapy ban took effect in 2022, while the city of Eau Claire, in Van Orden’s district, prohibited the practice in 2018. Meanwhile, at a June candidate forum in Platteville, Cooke said "no" when asked if the federal government should pass legislation to ban conversion therapy. Her answers prompted outrage from some progressive voters. "I find it interesting that not in one, but TWO forums you said you would leave conversion therapy up to the states to decide," one user wrote on Facebook. "That is not protecting the LGBTQ community." "I don’t know how you can say ‘Happy Pride’ if you aren’t willing to stand up for people you want to represent in Congress," another account replied. "If you are willing to sell out the LGBTQIA+ community for votes, who is next?" CHRISTIAN COUNSELORS CHALLENGE WISCONSIN CONVERSION THERAPY BAN AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING Amid the backlash, Cooke said she "misunderstood" the moderator's question and said she supported a federal ban on conversion therapy in a statement posted on a third-party account after the debate. During a July forum in Eau Claire, Cooke clarified, "I do not support conversion therapy whatsoever." Berge, who helped enact Eau Claire’s local conversion therapy ban, was clear throughout the candidate forums in denouncing the practice. "As a therapist, conversion therapy has no place in our society, in our culture," she said during the June event. Republicans sharply criticized Cooke’s reversal on conversion therapy bans. Van Orden's campaign argued Cooke, who counts Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., among her endorsers, flip-flopped on her stance while still trying to "portray herself as a moderate." "Rebecca Cooke is so desperate to appease the far-left woke mob that Wisconsin voters can’t be sure where she actually stands," Republican National Committee (RNC) spokesman Hunter Lovell told Fox News Digital. "She’s trying to be one candidate for liberal activists and another for everyone else," he continued. "Whether it’s caving to the far left or scrambling to rebrand herself for the general election, Cooke owes Wisconsinites an answer: Which Rebecca Cooke would show up in Congress?" Fox News Digital reached out to Cooke for comment. Cooke, a former Democratic consultant, fundraiser and small business owner, has consistently supported expanding LGBTQ rights during her previous two failed bids for Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District. In her third run for the seat, the repeat candidate is making clear that the Democrat-backed Equality Act — legislation that would make sexual orientation and gender identity protected classes under federal civil rights law potentially affecting women-only spaces and female sports teams — is a "centerpiece" of her campaign. She is also endorsed by the progressive Human Rights Campaign, which has advocated for sex change procedures for minors, including hormone therapy and puberty blockers. President Donald Trump comfortably carried the sprawling swing district by more than seven points in 2024, meaning Cooke would likely have to win over a segment of the president’s voters to prevail in November. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Cooke, who significantly outperformed former Vice President Kamala Harris, lost to Van Orden in the general election by just under three points in 2024, according to analysis from The Downballot. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the battleground contest as a "toss-up."
news.summary: Rebecca Cooke reversed her stance on a federal conversion therapy ban after progressive backlash, raising viability questions in the key swing district.

news.title: Rosie O'Donnell accuses CBS of giving Trump a 'bribe' by settling '60 Minutes' lawsuit
news.text: Liberal comedian Rosie O'Donnell accused CBS of "capitulating" to President Donald Trump on Monday during "The View" co-host Ana Navarro's podcast, saying the network's $16 million settlement of his "60 Minutes" lawsuit was a "bribe" that undermined an independent press. Appearing on "Bleep! with Ana Navarro," O'Donnell invoked former CBS late-night host Stephen Colbert, who used similar language while criticizing the agreement on his show last year. "[CBS] capitulated. They did exactly what Stephen Colbert said they did," O’Donnell said. "They gave him a bribe and it’s unforgivable." ROSIE O'DONNELL CLAIMS TRUMP HAS 'PTSD RESPONSE' TO HER AS BACKLASH ERUPTS O'Donnell said the agreement demonstrated why she believed the country no longer had a sufficiently independent media establishment to scrutinize the government. "We need a very vibrant, alive, independent media," O’Donnell said. "And we no longer have it in this country." The CBS case concerned the network's editing of an October 2024 "60 Minutes" interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump accused CBS of deceptively editing Harris' answer about Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to benefit her before the presidential election. Paramount Global and CBS settled the lawsuit in July 2025 for $16 million, covering legal costs and a contribution to Trump's future presidential library or charitable causes. The agreement contained no apology or admission of journalistic wrongdoing, and no money was paid directly to Trump. Trump’s legal team portrayed the settlement as a victory over the media. "CBS and Paramount Global realized the strength of this historic case and had no choice but to settle," a Trump legal spokesperson said at the time. SHARYN ALFONSI OUT AT ’60 MINUTES' AFTER FEUD WITH BARI WEISS, RIPS CBS FOR ‘CHILLING MESSAGE’ TO NEWSROOM During the discussion with Navarro on Monday, O'Donnell referred to Trump as a "convicted sexual rapist" while explaining why she moved to Ireland following his 2024 election victory. Navarro cautioned her against the description, prompting O'Donnell to turn to CBS and its settlement. Trump was not criminally convicted of rape. A civil jury found him liable for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll. ABC News separately agreed to pay $15 million toward Trump’s future presidential foundation or museum after anchor George Stephanopoulos repeatedly said Trump had been found liable for rape. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and CBS for comment, but did not immediately receive a response. TRUMP THREATENS TO ADD NY TIMES' 'TREASONOUS' IRAN WAR COVERAGE TO $15B DEFAMATION LAWSUIT Colbert criticized the CBS settlement with Trump on "The Late Show" last year because Paramount was awaiting federal approval of its multibillion-dollar merger with Skydance Media. "I believe this kind of complicated financial settlement with a sitting government official has a technical name in legal circles. It’s ‘big fat bribe,’" Colbert said. CBS announced three days later it would cancel "The Late Show" at the end of the 2025-2026 season, calling the move a financial decision unrelated to Colbert's content or other developments at Paramount. "It is not related in any way to the show’s performance, content or other matters happening at Paramount," CBS said in a July 2025 press release. Colbert hosted the program's final episode in May. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Federal Communications Commission approved Skydance’s $8 billion acquisition of Paramount three weeks after the settlement. The merger closed in August 2025. Paramount maintained during the proceedings that Trump’s lawsuit was "completely separate from, and unrelated to, the Skydance transaction and the FCC approval process."
news.summary: Rosie O'Donnell said CBS gave President Donald Trump a "bribe" with its $16 million "60 Minutes" settlement, echoing Stephen Colbert's criticism of the deal.

news.title: The GOP’s 2026 Trump problem, in 2 charts
news.text:
There has been plenty in President Donald Trump’s second term that’s proven politically unpopular.

But when it comes to what’s most significant for the upcoming midterm elections — and most problematic for Republicans trying to defend their congressional majorities — two charts tell the tale as well as anything.

Both feature a remarkably steady decline for Trump’s fortunes. And both now show him worse off than ever before.

The latest numbers come from new polling from CBS News and YouGov, which have frequently polled views of Trump’s handling of the economy over the last 18 months.

They also come as Trump headed to Michigan, a key battleground state, on Monday to promote his economic agenda.

Trump’s neglect on inflation

Early in Trump’s second term, the percentage of Americans who said the administration wasn’t focused enough on lowering prices was already high.

Back then, it hovered in the mid-60s, when the president seemed more focused on tariffs than kitchen table issues and inflation.

But the percentage of Americans who think the administration is not focused enough on lowering prices has risen steadily since then. And now, in the first poll asking the question since the start of the Iran war in late February, it’s up to 78 percent.

Just to underscore, that’s nearly 8 in 10 Americans who say the Trump administration has neglected what might well be the single most important issue to voters. It often seems difficult to get 7 in 10 Americans to agree on much of anything politically, but this is an even larger majority than that.

The percentage who say the administration hasn’t focused enough on this issue also includes 85 percent of independents and even a clear majority of Republicans (58 percent).

All three findings are new highs for Trump’s second term.

The poll question didn’t focus on Trump himself — it just asked about the administration — so maybe respondents had unnamed bureaucrats in mind rather than the president himself.

But this is a reflection of Trump’s presidency. And what’s most stunning is how steady it’s been. Trump hasn’t been able to do anything to temporarily juice the numbers in his favor. It’s a negative trajectory, with no end in sight.

The ‘financially worse off’ number

Ronald Reagan famously asked during his 1980 campaign against then-President Jimmy Carter, “Are you better off than you were four years ago?”

When it comes to Trump’s stewardship of the economy over the past 18 months, the answer to that question is not an encouraging one for Trump and the GOP.

The CBS poll has regularly asked whether Americans felt Trump’s policies were making them “financially better off” or “worse off.” And as with the first chart above, things have gone from bad to worse.

While 42 percent of Americans said Trump was making them financially worse off back in March 2025 — before Trump’s global tariffs were announced — that number has steadily climbed to 58 percent today.

Over the same span, the percentage saying Trump’s policies have made them better off has dropped from 23 percent to 13 percent.

So Trump has gone from 19 points underwater to 45 points underwater on that question.

What should sting more for Trump is that this was arguably one of the main reasons he was elected. Even as Americans had reservations about his personal character, they generally saw him as preferable on dealing with the economy.

In fact, CBS polling on the eve of the 2024 election showed 44 percent of registered voters expected Trump’s policies to make them better off. That was significantly more than the 30 percent who said the same of Democratic nominee Kamala Harris.

But today, just 13 percent of Americans say Trump has accomplished that.

And to be clear, this isn’t just Americans saying they’ve become worse off; they’re saying that and blaming Trump’s policies for it.

That was the danger of Trump effectively taking full ownership of the economy via his tariffs and the Iran war. And as the 2026 midterms get closer, there is no sign that either of these trends will get any better for the GOP.
