news.title: Donald Trump ordered to hand over financial records in £7.5 billion BBC lawsuit setback
news.text: Donald Trump has suffered a damning setback in his defamation case against the BBC after a judge ordered him to hand the broadcaster years of closely guarded financial records. The ruling means the US President, who has fought for decades to keep the details of his business empire secret, must disclose documents showing the value and financial performance of his companies. The BBC demanded the records as part of its defence against Trump’s $10 billion - £7.5 billion - lawsuit over a misleadingly edited Panorama documentary covering the January 6 riots. US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett indicated this would be her ruling last week - and it has now been made formal. She has ruled that the US leader could not claim the programme had caused massive damage to his businesses and personal brand while refusing to provide the evidence needed to test his allegations. The Donald J. Trump Revocable Trust, which owns virtually all his properties and businesses, has been ordered to begin handing over financial documents within ten days. It must then continue producing records every week until the process is complete. The Florida judge restricted the disclosure to documents dating from January 1, 2023, to the present, rejecting Trump’s attempt to block the BBC’s subpoena. The order represents a huge victory for the corporation, which apologised for the Panorama edit but refused to pay compensation. It also creates the prospect of intense scrutiny of financial information that the President has spent much of his public life trying to shield from rivals, investigators and the American public. Trump’s lawyers argued that the trust was not a party to the lawsuit and claimed the BBC’s requests were unreasonable, disproportionate and excessively burdensome. But Judge Lett said the scale of the disclosure sought by the broadcaster reflected the sweeping nature of Trump’s own claims. The president has alleged the programme caused “extensive economic harms,” “injury to [his] business and personal reputation”, and “massive economic damage to his brand value and significant damage and injury to his future financial prospects.” His lawsuit also claims there was “direct harm to his professional and occupational interests, including, without limitation, the value of his brand, properties, and businesses, and severe diminishment and tarnishing of his reputation as a politician, leader, and businessman in the eyes of the American public and around the world.” The judge said that because virtually all the properties and businesses Trump claimed had been damaged were held by the trust, its records were directly relevant to the case. She also said the BBC’s ability to examine the financial evidence was especially important because Trump was demanding damages of up to $10 billion. The dispute began with a 2024 Panorama documentary about Trump’s speech before his supporters attacked the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, in an attempt to stop the certification of Joe Biden’s election victory. The programme showed Trump saying: “We’re gonna walk down to the Capitol and I’ll be there with you and we fight. We fight like hell, and if you don’t fight like hell, you’re not gonna have a country anymore.” However, the passage had been created by joining remarks made at different points in the speech. Near the beginning, Trump said: “We’re gonna walk down, and I’ll be there with you, we’re gonna walk down, we’re gonna walk down any one you want, but I think right here, we’re gonna walk down to the Capitol, and we’re gonna cheer on our brave senators and congressmen.” His statement, “And we fight. We fight like hell. And if you don’t fight like hell, you’re not going to have a country anymore,” came towards the end of the address. The BBC accepted that the edit had created a misleading impression, apologised and said the documentary would not be broadcast again. But it refused to pay Trump compensation and maintains that the programme did not meet the legal threshold for defamation. The BBC’s decision to fight the case contrasts with the approach taken by several major American media companies which settled lawsuits brought by Trump rather than face a lengthy court battle. Disney, the owner of ABC News, agreed to pay £11.3million towards Trump’s future presidential library after presenter George Stephanopoulos wrongly said he had been found liable for rape. The company also agreed to pay £750,000 towards Trump’s legal costs. Paramount later agreed to pay £12million to settle Trump’s lawsuit over the editing of a CBS interview with his 2024 presidential election opponent, Kamala Harris . Paramount denied wrongdoing, but the settlements prompted warnings that large media companies were capitulating to legal and political pressure from Trump. The BBC has refused to take the same course and is instead contesting his allegations in court. Trump could appeal the disclosure order or reduce his claims of damage to his businesses to limit the financial evidence he must produce. The case is due to go before a jury in Miami in February 2027.
news.summary: A judge has ordered Donald Trump to disclose years of closely guarded financial records to the BBC after he claimed its Panorama documentary caused up to £7.5billion in damage to his businesses and brand

news.title: It’s not the left rising. It’s the center falling.
news.text:
Welcome to the first edition of The Midterms, Actually. Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one thing I’m thinking about — a big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries — and one thing I’m hearing, from a voice on the ground. You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every week. Let’s get into it.
One big idea
There are two ways of looking at the current divides within the Democratic Party. The first — and more dominant — narrative is that the party’s left wing is on an upward march, one that began with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s election in 2025 and has continued through this year’s Democratic primary season.
The second, and I believe more accurate, explanation is that the party is rudderless — an ideological fight to be settled in the next presidential election — and that the left’s success in New York City, Colorado, and even Maine (before Graham Platner’s campaign collapsed) grows out of a void left by a bigger, less-talked-about story: an establishment in free fall, on the wrong side of fundamental shifts across its own rank-and-file base.
The difference between those interpretations is fine, but important. I don’t think the Democratic base agrees with every position articulated by successful left-wing candidates — like “all deportations are wrong” (as NYC’s Darializa Avila Chevalier told me) — or have suddenly become committed democratic socialists. But I do think the left is on the right side of the gateway issues the base is currently prioritizing: a working-class-led affordability agenda, a skepticism of artificial intelligence, and a moral opposition to President Donald Trump’s war against Iran and to Israel’s campaigns of violence in Lebanon and Gaza. Those issues, more than any others, have defined the Democratic Party’s internal battles since 2024.
Progressives have also benefited from a moderate wing that, in many cases, has yet to lay out an affirmative vision. After the signature policies of the Biden administration flopped as political motivators, the center has seemed frozen in time, unable to offer its own blueprint for the electorate’s concerns (“abundance” aside). When I sat down with Third Way president Jon Cowan, he had no trouble assailing Hasan Piker, Abdul El-Sayed, or any number of the party’s most prominent progressive figures. But when I asked whether Third Way was actually responding to the clear shifts among the electorate — on Medicare-for-all, on abolishing ICE, on foreign aid to Israel — his answer was far less sure.
Cowan on America, Actually:
> We’ve never said that there’s a problem with Hasan Piker because he advocates for Medicare-for-all. … I think Medicare-for-all is still very problematic as a political issue, and if someone were nominated for president on the Democratic ticket and they were for Medicare-for-all, I think it would be a major barrier to getting elected. But that’s not our beef with Hasan Piker at all.
It was the same evasion whenever the conversation turned from the messengers to the message. In a recent interview with US Rep. Jim Clyburn — the powerful South Carolina Democrat who has endorsed US Rep. Haley Stevens’s Senate run in Michigan — he bluntly defended insider politics, insisting party leadership was not at fault for the 2024 result. The blame, he told me, belonged to the Black voters who hadn’t turned out for Kamala Harris.
Clyburn on America, Actually:
> When the white vote turned out 71 percent two years ago, and the Black vote turned out 59 percent, you tell me whose fault that is. … If that 59 percent had been 69 percent, she would’ve won.
When I asked him directly whether the argument was that Black voters had let Harris down, he didn’t hesitate: “In many instances, absolutely.” It is a remarkable thing to hear from a member of leadership — the base failed us, not the other way around — and it is exactly the instinct that has the establishment on its back foot.
This is why I think it matters to read the Democratic Party’s post-2024 convulsion as a story of establishment collapse rather than left-wing ascension. Stevens, Clyburn, and the party’s leadership would prefer to make this a referendum on the left — on the acceptability of its candidates and its media figures. But the base is communicating something else: a lack of confidence in the center, and in a version of establishment politics that prizes seniority and loyalty over voters’ values. Establishment collapse also explains the Democratic results that don’t fit neatly on the moderate vs. progressive binary: like Attorney General Phil Weiser’s victory in Colorado or whatever is happening in the Wisconsin governor’s race.
The center’s other problem is that its core general-election pitch — we may not thrill you, but we’re not Trump — is losing relevance the weaker that Trump looks politically. I spent a night at Trump’s UFC event on the White House lawn in June, an evening engineered to speak to the young men who broke his way in 2024, and found plenty of them cooling. “He was promising lower prices on everything,” one told me. “We didn’t know wars were gonna start.” Even the MAGA operative Jack Posobiec conceded that “the numbers are softer today, there’s no question about that.”
When the opposition’s own coalition is cracking, branding yourself as an inoffensive vessel who can gather up the most anti-Trump voters looks less compelling. The establishment needs an affirmative reason to be chosen — and it hasn’t found one.
So here’s my amendment to the narrative of the moment: The story isn’t a left-wing party discovering its confidence. It’s an establishment losing its own — and a base voting, in New York, in Colorado, and soon in Michigan and Wisconsin, on how much faith it still has that the center will name what it actually wants and fight for it. 
What I’m hearing: A Michigan reporter’s take on the Democratic Senate race
I reached out to Samuel Robinson, a reporter for the state’s oldest Black newspaper, the Michigan Chronicle; he also has a Substack, Detroit One Million. Robinson is based on Detroit’s east side, and he’s someone I’ve known for a while, as we’re both members of the National Association of Black Journalists. 
Both the Democrats’ moderate and progressive wings have invested so much in the state — it’s become the proxy war in the party’s fight over its future. What is it about Michigan that you think has made the stakes so high? 
Stakes are high because of the control of Congress. But also, Michigan is like a microcosm of America. It swings back and forth every four, eight years. But our US Senate seats have been held by Democrats since 1992. Republicans say they’re going to spend a ton of money to flip the seat being opened by Gary Peters retiring. Women moderates (Dana Nessel, Gretchen Whitmer, Jocelyn Benson) won big in 2018, and eight years later, all three to some degree have disappointed their own voters. Dems had a legislative trifecta from 2022 to 2024, and many people feel like Dems let down Black residents who got them elected in the first place. 
That’s one thing that unites the Black progressives and the Black establishment: Members in both camps feel the Democratic Party hasn’t done enough. 
How would you describe the difference between a Haley Stevens supporter and an Abdul El-Sayed supporter? 
Haley supporter — usually older; the young people I’ve met who support her typically come from wealthier backgrounds. Haley supporters are usually not involved in politics or people who keep up with national discourse. Haley supporters are worried about the gutting of the Voting Rights Act. They are worried about Trump nationalizing elections or not leaving the White House after ’28.
Abdul supporter — usually younger; the older people I’ve met who support him often acknowledge they are in the minority of their peers. The younger people who support him are all over the place in terms of their backgrounds — rich, poor, highly educated, no college. He has the support of most young people under 35. They are mostly worried about sending American taxpayer dollars to Israel, and the influence of AIPAC. I hear more about that than I do Medicare-for-all. 
Stevens has sought to capitalize on El-Sayed’s perceived weakness with the Black vote. How real do you think that vulnerability is? 
Abdul struggles with certain Black voters mostly because they don’t know who he is. I’ve heard from countless people who have said something to the degree of, “I don’t know enough about him.” He received media attention as the Detroit and Wayne County health director, but not enough for people to feel it. Most people know that he ran for governor in 2018 with no experience. People see Haley Stevens ads and mailers. Most Black voters aren’t on Twitter.
I saw this post on X where you were talking to a Stevens supporter who expressed some pretty bigoted claims about El-Sayed’s candidacy. How widespread is that sentiment? When I was reporting on Mamdani’s election in New York City, it was clear that there was anxiety among the Black political class that the rise of Asian, Latino, Muslim communities could displace them. Is that fear at play here? 
The race is definitely a tension point between Wayne County’s Black and Muslim population. Many who have shared with me similar sentiments will point to the anti-Black racism and exploitation of our community at the hands of Arab gas station and liquor store owners. That resentment builds up and then bubbles over in a race like this. We certainly live amongst each other, like off Seven Mile on the east side, where Bengali families and Black families live side by side as next-door neighbors. But there’s a resentment that goes both ways.

March 2, 2018: Rev. Billy Graham

“America’s Pastor” Billy Graham became only the fourth private citizen to lie in honor in the Capitol rotunda. Trump attended the service, alongside Melania Trump and Pence among others. Trump delivered brief remarks at the service, praising Graham for his devotion to Christianity.

Dec. 5, 2018: Former President George H.W. Bush

Trump joined all other former presidents at George H.W. Bush’s funeral, although he did not deliver a eulogy or speech. Trump paid respects in the Capitol rotunda and declared a national day of mourning. Trump said in a post on X that “this is not a funeral, this is a day of celebration.”

news.title: Talarico leads Paxton by 5 points in new poll of Texas’ U.S. Senate race
news.text:
WASHINGTON — The latest survey of the U.S. Senate race from Texas Public Opinion Research shows Democrat James Talarico leading Republican Ken Paxton, 45% to 40%, marking the Austin state representative’s largest lead in any public poll taken during the general election period.

Since Paxton locked up the GOP nomination in late May, polling of the contest has found a neck-and-neck race with neither candidate able to break 50%. But TPOR’s poll found Talarico leading among voters who do not have a college degree — a group that has consistently favored Republicans in Texas and across the country — and dominating among independents, less than a quarter of whom said they planned to vote for Paxton. The attorney general also had weaker Republican support than in other recent surveys, with nearly one in five GOP voters saying they were undecided or would vote for Talarico.

TPOR labels itself as a nonpartisan public opinion research group. It is directed by Democratic strategist Luke Warford.

The group surveyed 1,048 likely voters between July 15 and July 17, and has a margin of error of +/- 3.4 percentage points. Of those poll respondents, 53% voted for Donald Trump and 42% voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, making the sample only slightly bluer than the 2024 electorate, which favored Trump by a 14-point margin in Texas. Trump carried Texas by 5.6 percentage points in 2020, two years after the last midterm held during his presidency.

TPOR’s previous poll, fielded just after the May 26 runoff in which Paxton defeated Sen. John Cornyn, found Talarico leading 47% to 44%.

Texas’ U.S. Senate race figures to be one of the most closely watched and expensive contests in the nation. Democrats have not won a statewide race in the Lone Star State in over 30 years, but they believe a combination of Trump’s lagging approval ratings, Paxton’s ethical baggage and Talarico’s fundraising and populist messaging could deliver the victory that has eluded them for decades.

Republicans are taking the threat of Talarico seriously but nevertheless believe that, as the bitter primary between Paxton and Cornyn fades from memory and they highlight Talarico’s progressive views on social issues, Republicans will coalesce behind the attorney general. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the race as “Lean Republican.”

Paxton’s 40% vote share is the lowest he has received in a public poll post-runoff. Other surveys have found Republicans were consolidating behind him. But the TPOR poll had Talarico winning 7% of self-described Republicans, and an additional 12% remained undecided. Meanwhile, only 1% of self-identified Democrats indicated they would vote for Paxton, and 6% were undecided.

For comparison, a New York Times/Siena poll of the Texas contest fielded in June, which found the overall result tied at 47%, found Talarico winning 5% of Republicans and only 4% unsure.

Perhaps the biggest outlier was Talarico’s lead among non-college-educated voters, who favored the Democrat by nine percentage points — 45% to 36%. He led by 1 percentage point among those with at least a bachelor’s degree.

In recent elections, education has been one of the most reliable predictors of how people vote, with a sharp partisan dividing line between those with and without degrees. Exit polling found that Republican Sen. Ted Cruz beat Democrat Colin Allred by 18 percentage points among non-college-educated Texans in 2024. Even in 2018, when Democrat Beto O’Rouke came within 3 percentage points of victory, Cruz still won that bloc by a 6-point margin, exit polls found.

In the New York Times/Siena poll, Paxton had an 8-point lead among voters without a degree, and in TPOR’s own poll in May, Paxton led by a whopping 21 points among that group.

Other results hewed closer to recent polling of the race. The TPOR poll found Talarico leading heavily among Black and Latino voters, while Paxton maintained a strong lead with white voters. Black voters broke 71% for Talarico and 8% for Paxton, while Latinos preferred Talarico by a 66% to 20% margin. 

Paxton led among white voters, 53% to 33%.

Talarico’s polling lead owes to his strength with independents and non-college educated voters. The poll found Talarico garnering 43% of independents to Paxton’s 23%; 29% remain undecided. Among self-described moderates, Talarico’s lead is even more pronounced, with the Democrat ahead 54% to 20%.

The poll found that 14% of voters of all political stripes remain unsure about their pick. Among undecided voters, there is evidence Paxton has more room to grow: 19% of that bloc said they leaned toward the Republican, compared to 10% who leaned toward Talarico. Two-thirds reported being truly on the fence.

Elsewhere on the ballot, the TPOR poll finds Republicans leading in the contests for governor and attorney general — though both are also close.

In the governor’s race, incumbent Republican Greg Abbott was leading Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa of Austin by a 3-point margin, 45% to 42%. And in the open race to succeed Paxton as attorney general, Republican state Sen. Mayes Middleton of Galveston was up 39% to 38% over Democratic state Sen. Nathan Johnson of Dallas, well within the margin of error.

Both of those spreads would represent Democrats’ best performances for those offices in decades. But the high level of undecided voters in all three contests — U.S. Senate, governor and attorney general — suggest lots of room for movement in the less than 12 weeks remaining until Oct. 19, when the polls will open for early voting.

news.title: 10 House Seats Democrats Could Flip in 2026—And What the Polls Say
news.text: Democrats enter the final stretch of the 2026 midterm cycle needing a net gain of just three seats to reclaim control of the House of Representatives. That relatively small number has placed renewed attention on a handful of competitive Republican-held districts that could determine which party controls Congress in January next year. When approached for comment, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) pointed Newsweek toward the dozens of offensive targets featured in its "Districts in Play" program, arguing that Republicans are defending a historically narrow House majority and facing political headwinds in several suburban and swing districts. Publicly, the DCCC currently lists 46 districts as part of its broader battlefield. But which of those Republican-held districts look most vulnerable right now? To answer this question, Newsweek has ranked the 10 most competitive GOP-held seats using their 2024 House margin, presidential voting patterns, and incumbency status before reviewing the latest polling in each contest. How Rankings Were Calculated The ranking gives the greatest weight to the House margin, while also accounting for the district's broader partisan lean. Districts with narrow House victories and closely divided presidential results rank highest. Open seats receive a boost because they lack the advantages of incumbency, while districts that voted heavily for President Donald Trump rank lower even if the House race itself was relatively close. Public polling was then reviewed to assess whether current data is consistent with those underlying electoral fundamentals. Democratic strategists broadly agreed with the districts identified in Newsweek's analysis, with a DCCC operative describing the races on the list as "heavily contested" and among the most competitive House battlegrounds in the country, while arguing that many voters are increasingly focused on cost-of-living concerns rather than candidates' local profiles. Republicans reject the idea that these districts are easy Democratic pickup opportunities, with a Republican National Committee (RNC) strategist telling Newsweek that the party views each race as a distinct contest shaped by local political dynamics rather than national trends, arguing that many GOP incumbents have built strong local brands and remain well aligned with their districts. Democrats counter that voters are more focused on economic outcomes than incumbency advantages, particularly in districts where Republicans won in 2024 on promises to lower costs and inflation. A Democratic strategist told Newsweek that many Republican incumbents are now being judged less on their 2024 campaigns and more on whether voters believe the GOP has delivered on promises to lower prices and improve economic conditions. The GOP operative also said Republicans remain confident in districts carried by Trump in 2024 and expect the president's physical campaigning involvement and endorsement of candidates to help boost turnout among GOP voters, potentially offsetting the historical tendency of the president's party to struggle during midterm elections. They also said the GOP intends to concentrate resources on a relatively small number of competitive seats. With that in mind, here are the 10 Republican-held House seats that currently appear most vulnerable to a Democratic pickup. 1. Colorado's 8th Congressional District Colorado's 8th District remains one of the most obvious Democratic pickup opportunities in the country. Republicans won the 2024 House race by just 0.74 percentage points, while Trump carried the district by only 1.9 points. Republicans argue that incumbent Gabe Evans remains well positioned despite the district's narrow partisan divide. An RNC campaign operative told Newsweek that Evans' background as a Hispanic rancher resonates with the district's sizable Hispanic population and agricultural economy. Democrats have nominated state Representative Manny Rutinel after a closely watched primary. On June 30, Rutinel won the Democratic primary 62.8 percent against 32.5 percent for former state Representative Shannon Bird. With the nomination now decided, both parties are expected to pour resources into a district that was one of the closest congressional races in the country in 2024. Before the primaries took place, The Cook Political Report had the general race as a toss-up. 2. Arizona's 6th Congressional District Few Republican incumbents face a more consistently competitive district than Representative Juan Ciscomani. Trump carried Arizona's 6th by only about seven-tenths of a percentage point in 2024, while Republicans won the House race by 2.5 points. Democrats have now formally nominated former Marine JoAnna Mendoza to challenge Ciscomani after Arizona's July 21 primary, setting up one of the party's top pickup opportunities in the Southwest. A survey from the House Majority PAC—the Democratic-aligned spending group—conducted from June 8-11 among 500 likely voters, found Democratic challenger JoAnna Mendoza leading Ciscomani 47 percent to 45 percent. The margin of error was plus or minus 4.4 percent. A Republican-sponsored Ragnar Research Partners poll conducted March 12-14 among 400 likely voters found Mendoza leading 47 percent to 44 percent, with a margin of error of plus or minus 5 percentage points. When both Democratic and Republican-sponsored polls point in the same direction, strategists on both sides tend to take notice. Republicans also point to Ciscomani's incumbency as a key advantage. An RNC campaign operative told Newsweek the congressman has built strong name recognition in the district and can campaign on a record of bringing federal resources back to southern Arizona. 3. Pennsylvania's 7th Congressional District Representative Ryan Mackenzie won this district by just one percentage point in 2024, making it one of the narrowest Republican victories in the country. Trump carried the district by 3.2 points, but its recent electoral history suggests significant crossover voting remains possible. Democrats nominated retired firefighter and union leader Bob Brooks in May, setting up a closely watched contest against the first-term Republican incumbent. The most recent public poll, conducted by GBAO for House Majority PAC from June 29 through July 2, with a plus or minus 4.2 percentage point margin of error, found Democrat Bob Brooks leading Mackenzie 47 percent to 43 percent among 550 likely voters. 4. Arizona's 1st Congressional District Open seats often generate some of the most competitive races in the country, and Arizona's 1st District is no exception. The district voted Republican in 2024 but remains politically divided and highly competitive. Democrats nominated former state Representative and emergency physician Amish Shah. Republicans appear to view the race as one of their strongest pickup opportunities on the map after Shah defeated Marlene Galán-Woods, the DCCC-backed candidate, in the Democratic primary. An RNC campaign source told Newsweek the party believes Democrats must now heal divisions and “dysfunction on their side” from the nomination contest, while Republicans have united behind former NFL kicker Jay Feely following his endorsement from Trump. The matchup also comes with an unusual personal connection: years before entering politics, Shah served as a physician for the New York Jets while Feely played kicker for the team. A GrayHouse survey conducted November 15-17, 2025, among 500 likely voters found Feely tied with a generic Democrat at 42 percent. The poll carried a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. A separate Clarity Campaign Labs survey conducted November 1-5, 2025, among 676 likely voters, with a plus or minus 2.92 percent margin of error, found a Republican leading a Democrat by one point, illustrating just how closely balanced the district remains. 5. Michigan's 7th Congressional District Michigan's 7th combines a narrow presidential margin with a relatively competitive House result, making it a natural battleground. Regardless of who emerges from the Democratic primary on August 4, it is expected to remain one of the most closely watched races in the Midwest. Unlike several other districts on this list, recent polling has tested actual potential general-election matchups. A Data for Progress survey conducted June 24-30 among 772 likely voters found Democrat William Lawrence leading Republican Representative Tom Barrett 48 percent to 46 percent. The survey reported a margin of error of plus or minus 4.1 percentage points. The same poll found Barrett leading former Ambassador Bridget Brink by one point and leading former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam by one point, suggesting a genuinely competitive district rather than one favoring either party decisively. 6. Virginia's 2nd Congressional District Trump carried Virginia's 2nd District by less than a point in 2024, making it one of the most closely divided districts in the nation. Republican Representative Jen Kiggans benefits from incumbency, but the district's narrow presidential margin keeps Democrats interested. Current publicly available race trackers do not show recent head-to-head surveys in the district. But even without recent public horse-race polling, the district's electoral fundamentals place it firmly among the most competitive Republican-held seats. 7. New York's 17th Congressional District New York's 17th may be the classic example of a ticket-splitting district. Former Vice President Kamala Harris narrowly carried the district in 2024, yet Republican Representative Mike Lawler won his House race comfortably. A House Majority PAC survey conducted by FM3 Research from June 27 through July 1 found Democrat Cait Conley leading Lawler 51 percent to 45 percent among 509 likely voters. The margin of error was plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Lawler has repeatedly demonstrated political strength in a district that leans slightly more Democratic at the presidential level, but the polling suggests Democrats believe they have a real opportunity to reverse that trend. 8. New Jersey's 7th Congressional District Representative Tom Kean Jr. remains one of Democrats' top suburban targets. Kean's reelection bid has been complicated by questions surrounding his 142-day absence from Congress earlier this year. After returning to the House on June 30, the New Jersey Republican revealed he had been hospitalized and treated for depression, having missed more than 140 votes during his absence. Trump narrowly carried the district in 2024, but its demographics continue to make it attractive territory for Democrats. A Z to A Research survey conducted May 24-26 among 430 likely voters found Democratic nominee Rebecca Bennett leading Kean 46 percent to 43 percent. The poll carried a margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. Although the polling was commissioned by Democratic-aligned group 314 Action, the results reinforce why national Democrats continue to prioritize the district. 9. Pennsylvania's 10th Congressional District No Republican-held district currently shows stronger Democratic polling than Pennsylvania's 10th. A Normington Petts survey conducted April 20-23 among 400 registered voters found Democrat Janelle Stelson leading Representative Scott Perry 51 percent to 45 percent. The poll carried a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. An earlier Public Policy Polling survey conducted November 18-19, 2025, among 549 registered voters found Stelson leading Perry by 4 points, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. The consistency of the polling gives Democrats reason for optimism, though Perry has repeatedly survived difficult races before. 10. Iowa's 3rd Congressional District Iowa's 3rd rounds out the top 10. The district trends slightly more Republican than several others on this list, but competitive House results and mixed polling keep it firmly in play. A Republican-sponsored Ragnar Research Partners survey conducted March 12-14 among 400 likely voters found Republican Representative Zach Nunn leading Democratic state Senator Sarah Trone Garriott 48 percent to 42 percent. The poll carried a margin of error of plus or minus 5 points. At the same time, a Change Research survey conducted October 23-27, 2025, among 638 likely voters found a generic Democrat leading a generic Republican 45 percent to 42 percent. The poll reported a modeled margin of error of 4.3 percentage points. Those competing indicators illustrate why Iowa's 3rd remains on virtually every Democratic target list despite its slightly more Republican lean. What Happens Next Democrats do not need to sweep these districts to reclaim the House. They need only a handful of pickups. While Republicans argue incumbency and local ties will help them hold many of these districts, Democratic strategists told Newsweek they believe the election is increasingly being shaped by household economics, with cost-of-living concerns likely to outweigh traditional measures such as name recognition or past electoral performance. Many of these races remain in their early stages. Candidate quality, fundraising, the national political environment and voters' views of Trump will all influence the eventual battlefield.
news.summary: Newsweek analyzed polling, election data and insights from Republican and Democratic strategists to rank key House battlegrounds.
news.author: Sam Stevenson

news.title: Republican and Democratic coalitions put to the test in unusual elections on Tuesday
news.text: Two races in politically disparate parts of the country set the stage for one of the most unusual split-screen election days of the year on Tuesday. Rep. David Scott’s death in April at age 80 created a vacancy in a heavily blue district encompassing the southern and eastern Atlanta suburbs of Stockbridge, Conyers and Snellville. With the general election ballot already decided, Tuesday’s contest will determine who will finish out Scott’s term. Scott was notably related by marriage to Braves slugger Hank Aaron. Across the country in South Dakota, Republicans vying for the Mount Rushmore State’s safely red governor’s seat have created the state's first gubernatorial runoff between incumbent Gov. Larry Rhoden and self-made millionaire bitcoin investor Toby Doeden. TRUMP’S GOP CLOUT FACES ARIZONA TEST WITH HOUSE MAJORITY, GOVERNOR’S RACE AT STAKE Rhoden originally took the reins in Pierre after President Donald Trump chose former Gov. Kristi Noem to be Homeland Security secretary in his second term. He was unable to garner enough support in the June primary to secure the nomination outright in his first statewide election as governor. South Dakota’s runoff is expected to be a classic establishment-versus-outsider race, with Rhoden heavily favored in the polls but Doeden hoping for a Sioux Falls-fueled upset. Minnehaha County, home to Sioux Falls, is a key county to watch Tuesday after helping propel Doeden to a first-place finish in the June primary. WATCH: LAWMAKERS REVEAL WHERE THEY STAND ON CONGRESSIONAL TERM LIMITS AFTER RECENT HEALTH SCARES Pennington County, on the state’s western side, will also be closely watched after contributing to Doeden’s top finish in June. In contrast to what is expected in Scott’s district in November, Republicans are heavily favored because South Dakota has not elected a Democratic governor since the 1970s. Then-Gov. Richard Kneip served nearly two terms before President Jimmy Carter nominated him as ambassador to Singapore. Gov. Harvey Wollman completed the final six months of Kneip’s term, and is the state’s last Democrat to hold the office. EX-NFL LINEBACKER POISED TO RETURN TO CONGRESS AFTER TEXAS RUNOFF WIN WITH JASMINE CROCKETT ENDORSEMENT Shifting back to the Deep South, Georgia Democrats are expected to hold Scott’s seat in the fall by a wide margin. Efforts to replace Scott grew in recent months, particularly among the party's progressive wing, as the 12-term, often-combative lawmaker drew increasing frustration from Democrats. FROM LOCKER ROOMS TO CONGRESS, JAY FEELY THE LATEST ATHLETE SEEKING TO TAKE LESSONS ON LEADERSHIP TO CAPITOL HILL Last year, Scott made waves in Washington media when he shouted expletives at a Politico photographer as he was wheeled through the Capitol by staff. "Who gave you the right to take my picture, a—hole," Scott shouted at photographer Francis Chung in late 2025. That demeanor was similar to what led Everton Blair to launch his primary bid against Scott, in what his campaign page calls a "voice for a new generation." Blair previously told Fox News Digital it was a run-in with Scott at a Gwinnett County town hall, where the lawmaker gave insufficient answers to questions and then reportedly became confrontational, that led him to explore a bid. Blair had said he would "love to just hear a little bit more of the congressional and legislative strategy, congressman, that you have for this administration, particularly as it pertains to safeguarding federal funds," according to Semafor, when Scott replied "hold on," before becoming agitated: "I don’t know who sent y’all, but we got these folks here who are providing answers. And I’m doing this. That’s what I’m doing," Scott said, according to the outlet. Blair responded by launching a primary bid, while remarking to Fox News Digital at the time that two other elderly Democratic members had recently died in office "at a time when every vote counts." The wave of millennial candidates seeking to replace aging Democrats was at the time dubbed the "Biden effect" — Democratic lawmakers retiring or facing potential primary challenges following the octogenarian Delawarean’s disastrous debate performance, which led to his decision to step aside for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Change can’t wait, and Democrats need a new bench of leaders who are committed to solving real problems for working people," Blair said in a previous press release. Meanwhile, Scott’s daughter is hoping to replace her late father in Congress, remarking that she wants to continue his legacy. "That is my thing, is to finish out his year strongly, make sure that this money gets down to the district, and just make sure the 13th district is taken care of, constituency-wise, and making sure the projects go into finalization," she told the Georgia Recorder, while adding she would retain her father’s staff locally and at the Capitol for added stability. "[W]hen he first got into politics, I wasn’t even born, so I ran for some type of office or campaign every two years of my life, so this is just my norm, I’m just picking up where we left off with him," she told the outlet. A third candidate, former Mississippi judge Carlos Moore, also criticized Rep. Scott’s tenure, telling the Mississippi Free Press he wants to be a "leader who actually shows up." Moore had been suspended from the bench for one year in 2024 after a bar tribunal found he mishandled a wrongful death settlement, according to the outlet. When asked by the press about the infraction, he pointed to Trump’s 34-count indictment in New York. He also pledged, if elected, to be a leader who understands "how to defend our democracy and Constitution" from the president. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The winner of Tuesday’s special elections will serve only until January. Georgia state Rep. Jasmine Clark, D-Tucker, won the Democratic nomination for the full term earlier this year and is heavily favored against Republican Air Force veteran Jonathan Chavez in November. Trump lost the district by about 43 points in 2024.
news.summary: Gov. Larry Rhoden faces outsider Toby Doeden in South Dakota's first-ever gubernatorial runoff while Georgia Democrats vie to replace Rep. David Scott.

news.title: Trump defends his sweeping tariffs and watches 'America First' drag races during Michigan stop
news.text:
ReutersU.S. President Donald Trump

MILFORD: President Donald Trump came to Michigan on Monday and argued that his economic policies have revived the auto industry and American manufacturing, even as some businesses contend that the sweeping tariffs he's imposed have actually hurt the state.Trump visited a sprawling General Motors facility in the Detroit suburb of Milford that is a testing ground for its vehicles. He pumped a fist after watching a trio of drag races that involved muscle cars and luxury vehicles like the Corvette Z06, Cadillac Escalade V, and EV Hummer - events the announcer promised were "all America First power."Also read: USTR's Greer says Trump's latest tariffs won't have an economic impactIt was the kind of thundering speed the president is expecting at an IndyCar race in Washington next month, which is part of America's 250th birthday celebrations.Live EventsIn a subsequent speech inside a design facility, the president cheered GM's plans to expand production domestically in coming years and declared himself a president who was standing up for auto workers "at long last.""I've done more for you than your parents, OK?" he joked.Michigan was one of the 2024 battlegrounds Trump flipped after it backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. But the state has seen parts of its economy affected by the president's tariffs, including on imported cars and auto parts. Automakers have long said tariffs increase the cost of doing business, which leads to higher prices for consumers.Company officials led Trump on a tour where he saw various GM models, including the latest versions of the Chevrolet Suburban, GMC Sierra and Chevrolet Silverado - the production of which he argued had been boosted by tariffs.At one point, POTUS grabbed a pen and signed the hood of a white Corvette that was made specifically for America's 250th birthday."They've come a long way," he said to reporters about the Detroit-based automaker during the tour. "It's amazing what tariffs are doing for GM." Trump said he's been good to the company but he declined to say more."The rest of the world doesn't love me, but that's OK," he said, alluding to tariffs. "It's called 'America first.'"Also read: Donald Trump demands Senate to cancel August break until it passes voting billTrump's visit previews Michigan's Aug. 4 primaryThe president's speech lasted more than an hour and was wide ranging - hitting on the economy, the war in Iran and the U.S. military operation that toppled the leader of Venezuela.He also touched on communism, crime rates, his administration's efforts to transform the nation's capital and even how carefully he treads to keep from tripping while on stage or deplaning from Air Force One.With early primary voting already underway, Trump called on stage Republican Reps. Lisa McClain, Tom Barrett and Tim Walberg, as well as gubernatorial candidate John James and Senate candidate Mike Rogers.Rogers is unopposed in the Senate primary, but the GOP gubernatorial contest pits James, who is backed by Trump, against Perry Johnson, a businessman turned politician who has launched unsuccessful campaigns before, including for president in 2024.Trump's new Canada tariffs could hurt MichiganA new round of steep import levies is taking effect on dozens of U.S. trading partners. news.text:
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Monday endorsed Maine’s Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, Troy Jackson, just two days after the state’s party used a hastily called nominating process to name him as the replacement candidate in a race seen as crucial for control of the chamber.

Jackson secured the Democrats’ nomination on Saturday to run against longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins. Party delegates held a special nominating convention for the post after Graham Platner, who won the June primary, withdrew from the race in the wake of sexual assault accusations that he has denied.

The last-minute scramble for a new candidate in a top-tier race was reminiscent of how Harris ascended to the Democratic presidential nomination two years ago.

She became the party’s nominee in August 2024 after President Joe Biden abruptly ended his reelection campaign following a disastrous debate performance against then-former President Donald Trump. Trump would go on to defeat Harris, winning every presidential battleground state.

In a fundraising email to supporters Monday, Harris said she relates to the hurried nature of Jackson’s candidacy and called on Democrats to support him.

“I know what it is like to step up to the plate with a short runway to Election Day. Troy will have just 101 days between his nomination for Senate and when voters in Maine will cast their ballots,” Harris said in the email.

Democrats are counting on a win in Maine to have a chance to take back control of the Senate. They also need to win three other Republican seats and to hold all the seats they currently have.

Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and former president of the Maine Senate, initially ran for governor during this year’s primary. He lost that race but quickly became the party’s preferred candidate to replace Platner, with whom he had campaigned before Platner’s candidacy fell apart.

Representatives for Jackson’s campaign and the Maine Democratic Party did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It was not clear whether Jackson had approached Harris for an endorsement or her statement of support was unsolicited.

Jackson’s campaign said in a statement earlier Monday that it is working on making up a fundraising deficit against Collins, who has raised more than $16 million. Jackson has raised $2 million since securing the nomination, the campaign said.

Jackson “is harnessing historic energy across the state to deliver the change Mainers have been demanding over Collins’ three-decade career in Washington,” the campaign said in a statement.

Republicans in the state were swift to mock Harris’ endorsement and drew comparisons to the fact that neither Harris nor Jackson won a party primary before becoming the nominee.

“She knows exactly what he’s going through,” said Blake Kernen, a spokesperson for Collins.

news.title: Trump uses stage at General Motors to launch midterms attack on Democrats
news.text:
MILFORD, Michigan – US President Donald Trump touted his record on investment, job creation and tax cuts on July 27 less than 100 days before the November elections, even as polls showed Americans increasingly souring on his handling of the economy.

In a campaign-style speech at a test facility of American automotive manufacturer General Motors in Michigan, Trump also lashed out at Democrats seeking to end Republican control of Congress, calling his political opponents “communists” to cheers from many in the audience.

“Jobs are up, inflation is down, our border is secure. Factories are opening at record levels. Investment is booming. Michigan is thriving. America is winning like never before,” Trump said in a speech that also touched on immigration, the Iran war, voting restrictions and transgender issues.

Presidents often speak at auto plants but it is highly unusual for them to turn speeches at factories into campaign rallies. GM declined to comment on the partisan nature of Trump’s speech.

The first 18 months of Trump’s second term as president have featured a series of policy-driven economic shocks, driven by an immigration crackdown, higher tariffs and a war with Iran that has boosted the price of oil and ​threatened global supply chains.

Polls show that the high cost of living remains the top issue for American voters heading into the midterm November elections, including in Michigan, a key swing state.

Trump’s attacks on Democrats reflected a theme he has increasingly embraced in recent weeks. With the Iran war exacerbating Americans’ economic concerns, he has sought to energise his political base by presenting Democrats as radicals bent on fundamentally transforming the country.

“We’re having the single greatest year we’ve ever had as a country. We’re not going to let these people destroy it,” he told an audience that included GM CEO Mary Barra.

During the speech, Trump falsely claimed that Democrats seeking office wanted to raise taxes to 80 per cent and abolish the police. He also described the US trade deficit as having declined by 71 per cent, though the actual number in 2025 was a 0.2 per cent decline.

Sceptical Michigan

Michigan voters have become more sceptical about Trump’s handling of the economy and trade, according to Bernie Porn, president and pollster at Epic MRA.

Trump’s job approval rating in the state has fallen to 33 per cent, with 61 per cent disapproving, while most voters say consumers – not foreign countries – are bearing the cost of tariffs.

“He’s got a serious problem going into the midterms because people don’t believe him and they don’t think he’s telling the truth,” Porn said of the Republican president’s problems in Michigan, where Epic MRA is based.

White House spokeswoman Liz Huston said Trump’s “America First” agenda has driven automakers to invest, hire and expand, calling it a pace of growth “not seen in decades”.

Trump defeated Democratic former vice-president Kamala Harris by roughly 1.4 percentage points in Michigan in the 2024 presidential election, flipping it back to Republicans after Democrat Joe Biden won the state in 2020.

Michigan will be a critical battleground in the fight for control of Congress, with an open Senate seat drawing national attention. The state’s Republican and Democratic voters will choose their nominees in an August primary.

The Senate race will test whether Trump’s strength among working-class voters can translate into broader political gains. Republicans are rallying behind former US congressman Mike Rogers, while Democrats are holding a competitive primary featuring US Representative Haley Stevens and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed.

Trump delivered his speech at GM’s Milford Proving Ground, the company’s vehicle-testing facility. Located about 65km north-west of Detroit, the site covers thousands of acres and includes test tracks, laboratories and specialised facilities for simulating real-world driving conditions.

Trump has used tariffs to push American manufacturers to move production to the United States.

GM plans to move production of the Chevrolet Blazer from Mexico, while adding Equinox production in the US to supplement existing capacity. REUTERS

news.title: Trump says he's done more for Michigan autoworkers than their parents
news.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump told Michigan autoworkers that he's done more to improve their lives than their own parents in a speech at a General Motors facility outside of Detroit less than 100 days from the midterm elections.

"I've done more for you than your parents, OK?" Trump said, speaking at GM's automotive testing facility in Milford, Michigan. "Your parents are good. I'm not going to knock your parents, but I have been better to you than your parents. That I can tell you, and they would agree with me."

Trump's remarks came as he blasted United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain for his union's endorsement of Democrats Joe Biden and later Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. "You wouldn't have an auto industry right now if they got elected," Trump said.

"I don't know what happened to the guy. Somebody said he got fired," Trump said of Fain, who remains UAW's president. "But I can tell you, it's the people that count. Those people love Trump."

Trump credited his tariffs on foreign automobiles for strengthening the U.S. auto industry. He said GM's truck and SUV production is up by 20% in 2026.

But employment in autos and auto parts is down about 4% nationally from December 2024, the month before Trump took office, according to preliminary seasonally adjusted June numbers from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. In Michigan, total manufacturing jobs fell 2.5% during the same period.

Trump has long touted his support among working-class union members, including autoworkers, who have bucked their union's Democratic endorsements to vote for him. His strong backing among blue-collar white voters helped him carry Michigan in the 2024 election four years after losing the state to Biden.

100 days until the midterms: Dems lead in polling, GOP in redistricting

Trump reveals purchase of 250 Escalades for presidential motorcade

In his 65-minute speech, Trump slammed Democrats as extreme "communists" and claimed the United States has had "the single greatest year we've ever had as a country." He also revealed his administration recently ordered 250 Cadillac Escalades for the presidential motorcade.

"We look sharp in those Escalades. Our guys are very spoiled. They like the Escalades, so do I," Trump said. "They're making literally 250 of them, and it was about time."

It was not immediately clear how much the government spent to purchase the vehicles or when they will they will join the motorcade.

Trump's second term: President Trump visits Michigan amid fight over GOP nominee for governor

Trump sought to use his trip to Michigan to boost the candidacy of Mike Rogers, who is expected to be the state's Republican nominee for U.S. Senate after losing narrowly to Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin in the 2024 election. Rogers is likely to face either Rep. Haley Stevens or Abdul El-Sayed as the Democratic Senate nominee.

Michigan's party primaries are Aug. 4.

"Imagine if, Mr. President, you have a senator that cares as much about manufacturing, especially in Michigan, as you do," Rogers, a former Republican congressman, said after Trump welcomed him and other Michigan Republican candidates on stage.

Rogers later added: "When I get back there, Mr. President, if you haven't gotten it done, we're going to pass the SAVE Act," the president's long-stalled bill that seeks to overhaul voting in federal elections.

Trump, who won the White House on a promise to lower the cost of living, also has seen his approval ratings sag, meaning kitchen table issues could be a liability for Republicans trying to hold control of Congress in the Nov. 3 elections.

“We’re happy to have the president here, campaigning with Republicans. We think it highlights the fact that the only thing they care about is Donald Trump and refuse to stand up to him," said Curtis Hertel, chairman of the Michigan Democratic Party. "It’s good for us every time the president is here because he’s incredibly unpopular.”

The US and Canada have squabbled over a new border bridge

The Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s sweeping tariffs, but his administration has tried to find ways around that, including by arguing that he can impose them on Canada because that country is discriminating against American exports of products including automobiles.

But Trump’s latest round of tariffs came after he voiced frustration with Canada for having retaliated and imposed its own levies on U.S. imports in response to Trump’s initial tariffs last year. Trump launched the first round after alleging Canada should do more to stop fentanyl smuggling.

It is Trump's third trip to Michigan in his second term.

In January, he visited a Ford plant in Dearborn and addressed the Detroit Economic Club, offering a defense of tariffs even as auto industry leaders blamed them for increasing the cost of doing business.

The president marked his second term's first 100 days with a rally in Warren, where he mostly mentioned grievances left over from the 2024 campaign,

His latest visit coincides with tensions between his administration and Canada that have marred the opening of a new bridge linking Detroit and Windsor, Ontario.

Canada on Friday held its own event hailing the opening of the $4.7 billion Gordie Howe International Bridge instead of a planned celebration with officials in the U.S. after Trump announced the new Canadian tariffs.

An earlier, joint ceremony had been set for June but was scrapped after Trump suggested the U.S. wanted a “better” deal on the bridge it co-owns with Canada.

That eventually led to an agreement on splitting tolls that was supposed to allow for the rescheduled joint U.S.-Canada celebration — until the new tariffs derailed that, too.

news.title: Chuck Todd suggests DNC primary calendar intended to thwart potential progressive insurgent candidate in 2028
news.text: Former NBC News host Chuck Todd said Monday that the Democratic National Committee's (DNC) primary calendar looked as though the national Democratic Party was trying to thwart a progressive insurgent candidate from breaking through in 2028. During his podcast, "The Chuck ToddCast," the ex-NBC host said the schedule looked like it was made to make life harder for a progressive candidate. "The more I study this map, the more I think, whether intentionally or simply by consequence — though I don't think there's any accidents in presidential politics — this calendar is intended to make life harder for an insurgent progressive. That's its intent," he said. "The sequence itself is the story, right?" he continued. "Opening with South Carolina and closing with Virginia, a state that has been very friendly to Democrats, but not very friendly to progressive Democrats, right? But the sequence here does tell you something: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan, Virginia — not a place that's home to many super progressive electorates, right?" KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY Todd said if Wisconsin or Iowa were included in the early primary window, progressives would be happier. The DNC's Rules and Bylaws Committee (RBC) voted to keep South Carolina as the first-in-the-nation primary on Friday. The panel also voted to allow Nevada, New Hampshire, Michigan, Virginia and New Mexico to hold primaries in the early voting window, before the rest of the states hold nominating contests starting ahead of Super Tuesday. Axios reported Sunday that progressives were frustrated by the South Carolina decision. A member of the RBC told the outlet, "the public is swinging left, and the establishment is trying to fight the winds of change." The member said putting South Carolina first could "shut down" a progressive candidate early, according to Axios. BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS The RBC member also said it was "not a strategy for winning the electorate," per Axios. However, the report included some pushback from South Carolina Democratic Party chair Christale Spain. "I hate that the narrative kind of seems like 'Well, a progressive can't win in the South,'" Spain, who also worked for Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2016 campaign, told Axios. "The work that you have to do in the South is retail politics." Spain also said that a candidate such as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez could "absolutely" win in South Carolina. The DNC did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Todd said during his podcast, "If I were to create a calendar that was going to do two things — make it much harder for a progressive to get the nominee and much harder for progressives to say the calendar was designed to stop a progressive from getting the nomination — this is the calendar I would come up with." He added that Virginia, the final state in the early primary window, would become "the last stand for the establishment to stop a progressive if indeed a progressive has the momentum." STATES MAY DEFY DNC PRIMARY CALENDAR AS 'NOBODY IS SCARED' OF KEN MARTIN, CNN REPORTER SAYS The ex-NBC moderator said that South Carolina has not been "very open" to progressive socialist campaigns. However, he said in a crowded race, 20% of the vote might be enough to get second place, citing Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and his previous percentage of votes when he ran for president, 26% in 2016 and almost 20% in 2020, finishing in second in South Carolina both times. Todd said that it was also possible the situation could benefit a progressive, as there might be multiple moderates trying to secure the moderate vote. "There might be multiple candidates trying to win over the more moderate vote, it splinters and a progressive consolidating the progressive support in the state — well, guess what? Twenty percent is a terrible number in a two-way race. Twenty percent might be a great number in a six-way race," he said. "Today’s vote shows that many party insiders have learned nothing from 2024. New Hampshire has a proven track record of testing our candidates with a rigorous, fair, and efficient process, yet those qualities did not prevail. This committee’s vote does not change the realities governing New Hampshire’s primary, which are beyond the control of both this committee and our state party," Buckley said. "Today’s vote moves the party further away from that objective."
news.summary: Chuck Todd said the DNC primary calendar, starting with South Carolina, appears designed to make life harder for a progressive insurgent candidate to break through in 2028.
